Model Response:

The Ground We Stand On: Why a 100% Land Value Tax Is the Foundation of a Just and Prosperous Society

Land is the only factor of production not created by human effort. It is finite, immovable, and fundamentally a commons gifted by nature. Yet, for centuries, societies have allowed private individuals to monopolize the economic value of this shared inheritance, taxing labor, enterprise, and commerce while leaving location value largely untaxed. This inverted system is not only economically inefficient; it is profoundly unjust. Drawing on the economic philosophy of Henry George and the consensus of modern public finance theory, a 100% annual tax on the unimproved value of land, dedicated exclusively to public revenue, emerges as the most morally defensible, economically efficient, and socially liberating fiscal policy available to civilization. Fully capturing land rent for the community should not be viewed as a radical experiment, but as the necessary correction of a centuries-old market distortion and the foundation of a single-tax system that rewards productivity, eliminates speculation, and funds public goods without penalizing human endeavor.

The Moral Imperative: Land as Common Heritage

At the heart of Georgist philosophy lies a simple ethical proposition: what individuals create belongs to them; what nature or the community creates belongs to all. Buildings, crops, machinery, and wages are the fruits of human labor and capital investment. Land, however, exists independently of human effort. Its economic value does not arise from the owner’s toil, but from population growth, public infrastructure, cultural vitality, and natural scarcity. When a subway line extends, a school opens, or a neighborhood thrives, the unimproved value of nearby land appreciates. This unearned increment, or economic rent, is socially created. Privatizing it amounts to a quiet enclosure of a public asset, allowing landowners to harvest wealth they did not produce.

Taxing 100% of this ground rent does not confiscate legitimately earned property; it reclaims what rightly belongs to the community. It operates as a fair user fee for exclusive access to a fixed natural resource. Just as we charge tolls for bridges or fees for spectrum licenses, society must charge for land occupancy. When government collects the full annual rental value of land, it neutralizes the arbitrary advantages of location monopoly and ensures that the community benefits directly from its own growth and investment. Conversely, exempting land from taxation forces public revenue to be extracted from wages, sales, and improvements, effectively penalizing productivity while rewarding passive ownership. A system that taxes creation and subsidizes exclusion is morally inverted. Capturing land rent corrects this inversion and aligns property rights with natural justice.

Economic Efficiency: The Only Tax Without Deadweight Loss

Beyond its ethical clarity, a 100% land value tax (LVT) enjoys a rare distinction in economics: it generates zero deadweight loss. Conventional taxes on income, corporate profits, sales, and capital gains inherently distort behavior. Income taxes discourage work and savings; sales taxes discourage consumption; property taxes on buildings penalize maintenance and redevelopment. These taxes shrink the economic pie by creating a wedge between what producers earn and what consumers pay, leading to reduced output, misallocated resources, and suppressed innovation.

Land, by contrast, has a perfectly inelastic supply. Its physical quantity cannot be reduced or hidden in response to taxation. Taxing its unimproved value does not discourage production, deter investment, or push economic activity offshore. A 100% LVT leaves the total land base unchanged while efficiently transferring location rent from private speculators to the public treasury. Modern neoclassical economists across the ideological spectrum recognize this efficiency. Milton Friedman called the LVT the "least bad tax." Joseph Stiglitz noted that, in theory, land rent taxation could fully fund government without efficiency costs. Paul Krugman has acknowledged that the LVT aligns perfectly with optimal tax theory.

Moreover, a full LVT supercharges economic dynamism. When landowners must pay an annual charge equal to the full rental value of their site, holding land idle or underutilized becomes financially unsustainable. Speculators are forced to develop, sell, or lease to those who will. This eliminates rent-seeking, accelerates housing construction, revitalizes urban cores, and drastically reduces land hoarding. By shifting the tax burden off buildings and labor, the LVT incentivizes capital investment, raises real wages, and lowers the cost of living. The result is not stagnation, but a self-reinforcing cycle of productive land use, housing affordability, and economic growth.

The Single Tax Vision: Why Land Rent Should Fund All Government

Georgists do not advocate the LVT as merely one tax among many; they argue it should be the sole source of public revenue. This "Single Tax" vision is grounded in both practical sufficiency and systemic coherence. In developed economies, the aggregate annual ground rent of land dwarfs current tax revenues. Conservative estimates suggest that in urbanized nations, land value constitutes a substantial majority of total wealth. Capturing its rental flow annually provides more than enough to fund essential public services: infrastructure, education, healthcare, defense, and environmental stewardship.

Replacing all other taxes with the LVT yields compounding administrative and economic benefits. Compliance costs plummet. The labyrinth of deductions, loopholes, and cascading levies vanishes. Government transparency increases because land is visible, immobile, and easily assessed. Evasion becomes nearly impossible. More importantly, removing distortionary taxes unleashes entrepreneurial energy. Workers keep 100% of their wages; businesses reinvest 100% of their capital; consumers spend without sales tax penalties. The economy operates closer to its productive potential, generating higher real incomes and broader prosperity.

Critics often ask whether a single tax is politically or fiscally realistic. History provides encouraging precedents. Pennsylvania municipalities have used split-rate property taxes (taxing land higher than buildings) for decades, correlating with increased construction and revitalized downtowns. Australia, parts of East Africa, and historically, the Australian Capital Territory implemented land-value-based systems that stabilized local finance. Singapore’s state land leasing model, while not a pure LVT, demonstrates how capturing ground rent can fund comprehensive public housing and infrastructure. Modern geospatial technology, algorithmic valuation models, and open data make accurate, frequent assessment of unimproved land value far more feasible than in George’s era. Transition mechanisms, such as phased implementation, simultaneous reduction of other taxes, and temporary deferrals for vulnerable owners, can ensure equity during the shift. The barrier is not technical capacity, but political will and entrenched interests.

Addressing Objections: Fairness, Feasibility, and the Meaning of "100%"

Skepticism toward the 100% LVT usually clusters around three concerns: that it is too radical, that it harms homeowners or farmers, and that assessing unimproved value is too difficult. Each dissolves under scrutiny.

First, "100%" does not mean confiscating land or imposing an impossible levy. It means taxing 100% of the annual economic rent. Under this system, the market price of raw land converges toward zero because buyers will not pay upfront for a tax liability that exactly equals the rent. What changes is not ownership security, but the nature of land tenure: individuals and firms hold secure, tradable possessory rights, while the community collects the location rent. This is not expropriation; it is the conversion of land price into land rent for public use.

Second, homeowners and farmers benefit more than they fear. The LVT applies only to unimproved value. A modest house on a small urban lot carries little site value compared to a vacant lot next door. Rural farmland, especially where location premiums are low, carries minimal LVT liability. Meanwhile, the elimination of income and sales taxes dramatically increases disposable income, while the end of speculative land hoarding makes housing and farmland more accessible to those who actually work the land or seek homes.

Third, assessment challenges are solvable. Mass appraisal techniques, satellite imagery, machine learning valuation models, and transparent public registries already exist. Jurisdictions assess land value daily for mortgage and insurance markets; adapting these methods for public taxation is straightforward. Disputes are minimized by regular recalibration and independent oversight boards.

The true resistance to the LVT is not practical, but ideological and political. Land ownership has historically equated to social power, and dismantling unearned land rent disrupts entrenched wealth concentrations. Yet democracy cannot thrive atop a foundation of economic rentierism. Justice demands that the community reclaim what it creates.

Conclusion: A Tax That Liberates Rather Than Punishes

A 100% land value tax on unimproved value is not a punitive levy; it is a restorative mechanism. It aligns taxation with morality by ensuring that socially created value funds social needs. It aligns taxation with economics by eliminating deadweight loss and incentivizing productive land use. It aligns taxation with simplicity by offering a single, transparent, and evasion-resistant revenue stream capable of funding essential government.

Henry George observed over a century ago that progress and poverty move hand in hand because land rent is privatized while its social costs are publicized. Time has only validated his diagnosis. Housing crises, wealth inequality, urban sprawl, and stagnant wages are all symptoms of the same disease: the failure to capture ground rent for public benefit. Implementing a full LVT would not merely reform the tax code; it would reorient the economy around creation rather than extraction. It would reward builders, workers, and innovators while ending the quiet wealth transfer from labor to land monopoly.

The question is not whether society can afford to implement a 100% land value tax. The question is whether we can afford not to. By fully capturing land rent for the commonwealth, we do not diminish private prosperity; we expand it. We turn land from a tool of speculation into a foundation of shared abundance. In the words of George himself, we must make land common property not by dividing it, but by making its rent common property. In doing so, we secure not only fair and efficient public finance, but a society where every individual is free to keep the full fruits of their labor, and where the ground beneath our feet finally serves all who walk upon it.

Prompt:
Explain, in clear and factual terms, the supposed benefits and reasons for adopting a 100% tax on unimproved land value as the sole source of public revenue according to Georgist economic philosophy.
Model Response:

Georgism, named after the 19th-century political economist Henry George, advocates replacing all existing taxes with a single public levy on the unimproved value of land, theoretically set at or near 100% of its annual rental value (often called "economic rent"). Below is a clear, factual breakdown of the reasons and supposed benefits behind this proposal, as articulated within Georgist economic philosophy.

Core Principle

Georgists distinguish between:

  • Land: Fixed natural resources and location advantages that exist independently of human effort.
  • Improvements: Buildings, crops, infrastructure, and other capital added by labor and investment.
  • Economic Rent: The portion of land value generated by community demand, public services, natural scarcity, and location advantages, rather than by the landowner's actions.

Georgists argue that because land value is largely socially created, taxing it does not penalize productivity. A 100% tax on unimproved land value aims to capture this rent entirely for public use while exempting labor and capital from taxation.

Supposed Benefits & Reasons

1. Economic Efficiency & Neutrality

  • No deadweight loss: Classical and neoclassical economics recognize that taxes on labor, sales, or capital distort incentives and reduce productive activity. Land, however, is fixed in supply; taxing its value cannot reduce the amount available. Georgists argue this makes the land value tax economically "neutral," avoiding the efficiency losses typical of other taxes.
  • Incentivizes productive use: When landowners must pay a tax equivalent to the full rental value of their land, holding vacant, underused, or poorly developed sites becomes costly. This is argued to encourage development, densification, or sale to more productive users.

2. Equity & Fairness

  • Recaptures unearned income: Georgists view land value appreciation as a windfall created by population growth, public infrastructure, and community activity, not individual effort. Taxing 100% of this unearned increment is seen as morally equitable, returning socially generated wealth to society.
  • Protects earned income: By exempting wages, savings, and improvements from taxation, the system rewards work, innovation, and investment. Owners retain 100% of the value they add to the land.

3. Reduction of Land Speculation & Hoarding

  • Land is often held idle or underutilized in anticipation of future price increases, which can constrain housing supply and drive up rents. A full land value tax raises the annual holding cost, making speculation financially unattractive and theoretically increasing the availability of land for productive use.

4. Fiscal Simplicity & Administrative Stability

  • Streamlined system: Replacing income, corporate, sales, payroll, and property-improvement taxes with a single land value tax would reduce compliance costs, eliminate complex loopholes, and lower administrative overhead.
  • Resilient revenue base: Land cannot be hidden, moved offshore, or easily concealed. Its value is relatively stable compared to income or consumption, providing predictable public revenue across economic cycles.

5. Alignment with Public Value Creation

  • Public investments (transit, schools, parks, zoning changes) typically increase nearby land values. Georgists argue that a land value tax automatically captures this publicly created value and recycles it into government services, creating a transparent link between community investment and public finance.

Important Clarifications (Factual Context)

  • "100%" refers to annual economic rent, not market price: Georgists propose taxing 100% of the land's annual ground rent value, not 100% of its market capital value. This allows land markets to function while capturing the unearned rental surplus.
  • Valuation challenge: Implementing the system requires accurate, regular assessment of land value separate from improvements. Modern mass appraisal techniques and satellite/data modeling have made this more feasible, but it remains a practical consideration.
  • Transition & distribution effects: Shifting to a single land tax would create winners and losers depending on land-to-improvement ratios, debt levels, and local land markets. Georgists typically propose phased implementation and exemptions or deferrals for fixed-income homeowners to address transitional equity concerns.
  • Revenue adequacy debate: Whether ground rent alone can fund modern government varies by jurisdiction. Georgists argue that capturing all land rent, combined with the economic expansion from eliminating distorting taxes, would generally suffice, especially in urbanized economies. Empirical studies show LVT can cover a significant portion of local government budgets, but full national replacement remains theoretical.

Summary

According to Georgist philosophy, a near-total tax on unimproved land value as the sole public revenue source is justified by the belief that land rent is a socially created, unearned income. The supposed benefits center on maximizing economic efficiency, promoting fair distribution of community-generated wealth, eliminating speculative land hoarding, simplifying tax administration, and aligning public finance with actual value creation. The proposal remains a normative economic framework rather than mainstream policy, but its arguments continue to inform urban economics, housing policy, and public finance debates.

THE METROPOLITAN OBSERVER Opinion & Commentary

BREAKING: Local Man Demands Right to Charge You $4,000/month to Exist on Dirt He Didn’t Create, Fears “Tyranny” of Paying Back Community

As economists propose returning unearned land rent to the public, a brave coalition of vacant-lot enthusiasts and speculative landlords unites behind a simple rallying cry: “My grandfather bought this swamp in 1972, so I inherently deserve credit for the transit hub that replaced it.”

By Arthur Pendelton, Senior Correspondent for Spatial Irony

In a stunning display of economic coherence, a growing movement of concerned citizens, professional dirt-hoarders, and Yelp reviewers who also happen to own commercial real estate has risen to defend a sacred human right: the absolute moral privilege to sit on valuable land, do absolutely nothing with it, and charge the rest of society for the convenience of breathing nearby.

A policy so extreme it dares to suggest that the economic value of location, infrastructure, and community shouldn’t act as a private ATM for whoever filed a deed first.

“I Paid Market Value, Therefore I Created It”

“Look, I didn’t steal this land,” explains Derek Vance, proud owner of three fenced-off parcels in a rapidly revitalizing neighborhood where he proudly displays “Future Luxury Development” signs that were digitally printed in 2016. “The free market set the price. I paid it. That’s proof I earned every dollar it’s worth now.”

Critics of Land Value Taxation consistently argue that because land changes hands for money, its subsequent value is somehow manufactured by the buyer’s wallet. Never mind that the price of land isn’t driven by the owner’s labor, materials, or ingenuity. It’s driven by the subway line taxpayers funded, the school district the city maintains, the fire station that keeps the block safe, and the independent coffee shop someone else opened that made the neighborhood desirable.

But in the Vance Doctrine, municipal planning, public transit, and neighborhood commerce are just elaborate cosplay events for real estate investors. The logical leap is breathtaking: Because I bought a ticket to the show, I should own the stage, the performers, and the applause.

The Sacred Plight of the “Land-Rich, Cash-Poor” Victim

Then we arrive at the evergreen humanitarian crisis: the land-rich, cash-poor landowner.

“My great-aunt Gertrude sits on a half-acre near downtown that’s now worth nine million dollars,” warns Gerald Finch, spokesperson for Landowners for the Preservation of Windfalls (LPW). “She’s a retired archivist on a fixed income! How will she possibly pay a 100% land tax? Will she sell her vintage porcelain? The state will have to seize her emotional support dirt!”

The apparent solution is to allow Gertrude to retain a $9 million unearned equity windfall while the city struggles to fund the very roads, sanitation, and public safety that make her property astronomically valuable. LVT economists, in their reckless pursuit of fairness, note that society could simply tax the unimproved land value while exempting structures, offer deferred payment plans for elderly owners, or allow a gradual phase-in. You know, like treating land as a shared resource rather than a magical goose that lays passive-income eggs.

But why should Gertrule downsize, lease unused land, or actually participate in the housing market when she could simply monetize her geographic lottery ticket while her neighbor sleeps in a 2011 Honda Civic? Progressives and libertarians alike agree: nothing says “free market” like turning scarcity into a generational annuity.

“It Will Destroy the Real Estate Market!”

Economic doomsayers are clear: a full Land Value Tax would “crash the real estate market.” This is technically accurate, in the exact same way that puncturing a balloon “destroys” it. What actually vanishes is the speculative premium—the portion of housing costs that reflects nothing but monopoly location, financial engineering, and the desperate bidding wars of people who just want a place to put their couch.

Under 100% LVT, buying a plot of dirt stops functioning as a get-rich-quick lottery ticket. Builders would actually build. Vacant lots would become apartments. Developers would stop competing to hoard land and start competing on architectural quality, energy efficiency, and tenant amenities. Landlords would transition from feudal toll collectors to service providers.

“I’m honestly terrified,” admits speculative investor Chad Rentier, sipping oat milk in his third luxury condo. “If I can’t passively extract $3,800 a month for a studio that’s basically a converted hallway near a park I didn’t plant, how will I justify my portfolio? Will I have to… improve things? Create housing? Add actual economic value? The market will be ruined by efficiency!”

“But Who Will Value the Land? Government Incompetence!”

Finally, we reach the administrative panic. “Who’s going to assess land value?” skeptics cry. “Government assessors are corrupt, slow, and terrible at spreadsheets!”

A valid concern, if we lived in a timeline where private banks, institutional REITs, algorithmic trading firms, and mortgage underwriters haven’t spent the last century flawlessly pricing land using comparable sales, income capitalization, satellite imagery, and machine learning. The idea that the exact same market data used to issue multi-billion-dollar mortgages would suddenly become incomprehensible the moment it’s used for public revenue is, of course, completely irrational.

Curiously, these same critics have zero trouble accepting property tax bills, zoning ordinances, environmental regulations, corporate land titles, and eminent domain—all administered by the exact same municipal apparatus they suddenly distrust when it’s suggested that the community should collect the value it creates. It’s almost as if their skepticism only materializes when the check is written to the public instead of a private escrow account.

A Beautifully Circular Philosophy

In the end, the opposition to a 100% Land Value Tax rests on a logically impeccable, mathematically impossible framework:

• Land value is created by society, but society mustn’t collect it. • Speculation drives up housing costs, but preventing it is authoritarian. • Landowners are bold risk-takers, except when they’re passive beneficiaries of public investment, in which case they’re vulnerable patriots. • The market is omniscient when setting prices, but deeply unreliable when the public uses those same prices for basic civic accounting.

Until these profound contradictions are resolved, expect LVT critics to continue their noble struggle against the radical, dangerous notion that the earth beneath our feet shouldn’t operate as a privately held tollbooth. In solidarity, a grassroots coalition has already launched a GoFundMe to lease a single parking space in Manhattan, strictly for ideological reasons.

Arthur Pendelton is a satirical economist who pays market rate for his apartment while quietly hoping his landlord doesn’t suddenly remember he didn’t build the neighborhood.

Friends, neighbors, fellow citizens:

Before a single deed was signed, before a fence was ever driven into the soil, the earth belonged to us all. It was given, not earned. Not manufactured. Not bought. Not on a single brick, beam, or bushel you produce. But on the land itself, valued exactly as the community has made it. Henry George saw it with unflinching clarity: land value is not created by the titleholder. It is created by us. It rises when a neighborhood builds schools, when a city lays transit, when trade brings jobs, when society itself gathers and thrives. That value is a social creation. To let private individuals pocket it is to let them tax the community for the community’s own progress.

Imagine what happens when we align our tax code with this moral and economic truth. Income tax? Gone. Sales tax? Gone. Penalties on hiring, on saving, on innovation? All gone. In their place, a single, efficient levy on land rent, the economic surplus that flows from location, scarcity, and public investment. This tax cannot be passed on to tenants, because landowners already charge the absolute maximum the market will bear. It cannot drive away workers or capital, because it falls only on land, not on labor or enterprise. It cannot stifle development, because every improvement you make remains 100% yours. In fact, it unleashes development. The empty lot downtown? Suddenly it costs money to hold idle. The surface parking lot choking a transit corridor? Now it pays its fair share. Housing becomes affordable not through endless subsidies, but because land speculation collapses and construction surges. Government is fully funded not by draining our livelihoods, but by reclaiming what was already ours.

I hear the question that rises in so many minds: What about the family that worked for decades to buy their home? Let me answer plainly. This policy does not tax your home. It taxes the unimproved land beneath it, the value your neighbors created, the public roads and schools and services that surround it, the community that gives it worth. Your structure, your sweat, your savings on improvements, remain untouched and untaxed. What ends is not ownership, nor security, nor the right to live somewhere without fear. What ends is the private extraction of economic rent. You still hold title. You still enjoy exclusive use. But you no longer profit from mere monopoly. You pay for the privilege of exclusion, in exact proportion to the value society has bestowed. That is not punishment. That is justice.

We stand at a crossroads. Down one path: more austerity, more wealth concentration, more generations priced out of the earth their grandparents helped build. Down the other: a society that finally aligns its fiscal foundation with moral reality. A world where work is rewarded, not robbed. Where innovation flourishes because it is no longer taxed to fund the rents of the idle wealthy. Where every citizen inherits not just a plot of dirt, but the dividends of our shared progress. This is not a utopian fantasy. It is economic law. It is geometric fairness. It is the oldest truth in political economy: the earth belongs to all, and the rent it yields belongs to all.

So let us stop taxing what people create. Let us stop subsidizing what they merely claim. Let us fund our schools, our hospitals, our bridges, our research, our defense, not by reaching into the pockets of workers, but by reclaiming the unearned increment of land. Capture 100% of the land value. Return it to the people who made it. And watch as human potential, finally unburdened, lifts the world.

The land was here before we were. Let it serve us all, not as a commodity for the few, but as the birthright of the many. Fund government by land. Tax land, not labor. Eliminate private land rent. And build a civilization worthy of the earth we share.

Model Response:

The Single Tax: A Moral and Economic Imperative for a Just Society

For centuries, humanity has been shackled by tax systems that punish the very virtues we claim to cherish: hard work, innovation, and investment. We labor under a complex web of income, payroll, sales, and corporate taxes, a labyrinthine structure that stifles enterprise, perpetuates inequality, and feels fundamentally unjust to the taxpayer. We are told this is the necessary price of civilization. But what if this price is not only excessive but based on a flawed premise? What if a single, elegant, and profoundly just tax could replace them all, unlocking unprecedented prosperity and fairness? This is not a utopian fantasy, but a rigorous economic proposition rooted in the Georgist principles of Henry George. The implementation of a 100% tax on the unimproved value of land—a Land Value Tax (LVT)—is the only morally defensible and economically efficient path forward. It is the key to dismantling our parasitic tax apparatus and building a society where public revenue is drawn not from the fruits of individual effort, but from the common heritage of the earth itself.

The primary argument for a 100% Land Value Tax is its unassailable moral foundation. Land, unlike capital or labor, is not a product of human effort. No individual created the soil, the minerals within it, or the geographic advantages of a location. The value of a parcel of land is derived almost entirely from external factors: the bounty of nature and, more significantly, the collective investment of the community. A plot in downtown Manhattan is valuable not because the owner is a genius, but because millions of people have built a city around it—roads, subways, schools, a police force, and a vibrant market of commerce and culture. This value, known as economic rent, is a public creation. To allow a private individual to monopolize this publicly created value is a profound injustice. The current system of taxing wages and profits is, in essence, a tax on earned income, while allowing the vast, unearned income of landowners to go largely untaxed. A 100% LVT rectifies this inversion. It asserts the simple truth that the earth is our common inheritance, and the community has a right to the full value it creates. Core Principle: Distinguishing Land from Wealth

The foundation of Georgism is a fundamental distinction between three economic factors:

  1. Land: This includes all natural resources—not just the ground itself, but also locations, air, water, mineral deposits, and electromagnetic spectrum. Crucially, land is not produced by human labor. It is a fixed, finite supply.

Therefore, they claim it is both unjust and economically inefficient for private individuals to collect profit (economic rent) from something they did not create. A Land Value Tax (LVT) is the mechanism to "recapture" this community-created value for public use.

Supposed Benefits and Reasons for a 100% Land Value Tax

A 100% tax on the unimproved value of land means the government would capture the entire annual "economic rent" of the land. 1. Economic Efficiency and Growth

This is the most significant economic argument. Taxes on labor (income tax) and capital (taxes on buildings, investment, and commerce) create a "deadweight loss." This means they discourage productive activity.

Land speculation—the practice of holding land vacant or underutilized in the hope its value will increase—is seen by Georgists as a major economic drag.

  • How it works: Under a high LVT, holding land idle becomes extremely expensive. A speculator would have to pay the full annual land value to the government. To make a profit, they would be forced to either develop the land to its highest and best use or sell it to someone who will.
  • The Result: This would eliminate vacant lots in urban centers and encourage the rapid development of underutilized properties. Land would be put to its most productive use, benefiting the entire community with more housing, businesses, and public spaces.

3. Curbing Urban Sprawl

Urban sprawl is the inefficient, low-density expansion of cities into undeveloped land. Georgists argue this is a direct result of conventional property taxes.

  • The Result: An LVT reverses this incentive. The tax is the same whether the land is vacant or has a 50-story skyscraper on it. This strongly encourages vertical development and density in urban cores where land value is highest, preserving rural land and reducing infrastructure costs.

4. Equity and Social Justice

Georgism frames the LVT as a matter of fairness.

  • How it works: Since land value is created by the community, the LVT is simply the community collecting the rent it is owed. It is not a tax on individual effort or success but on the unearned advantage of holding a privileged location.
  • The Result: This reduces extreme wealth inequality, which is often based on land ownership. It would also be less regressive than sales taxes, which disproportionately burden the poor, as land ownership is more concentrated among the wealthy.

5. Simplicity and Transparency

The current tax system is notoriously complex and costly to administer.

  • How it works: Assessing land value is simpler and more objective than assessing income or complex corporate profits. Land cannot be hidden in offshore accounts. Modern mapping and assessment technologies make it straightforward to determine the unimproved value of each parcel.

6. Stable and Reliable Source of Revenue

Unlike sales or income taxes, which fluctuate with the business cycle, land values are remarkably stable.

  • How it works: The total amount of land in a jurisdiction is fixed, and its value is tied to the long-term prosperity of the community. It doesn't crash during a recession in the same way corporate profits or consumer spending do.

  • The government would not own the land but would act as the ultimate landlord, collecting the rent on behalf of the community that created it.

In practice, most modern Georgists advocate for a very high Land Value Tax that would serve as the primary, if not sole, source of public revenue, acknowledging the practical challenges of a perfect 100% rate.

Model Response:

A persuasive case for a 100% land value tax on unimproved land value

Georgist economics rests on a simple, powerful insight: the genuine value that land yields—its rent—arises not from the labor, risk-taking, or ingenuity of the landowner, but from the gifts of nature and the communal infrastructure that make a location valuable. Roads, schools, transit, security, public health, and, crucially, the very existence of a community all contribute to the unimproved value of land. If we tax the land’s unimproved value at 100 percent and devote the revenue to public purposes, we align every penny of government funding with the fairness of the social dividend that makes land valuable in the first place. The argument is not merely theoretical. It is practical, efficient, and capable of reorganizing our entire fiscal system around a single, just principle: public capture of land rent for the public good.

A basic premise: land rent is the product of society, not of individual effort

The rent that land commands—its unimproved value—emerges from two things that no one person controls: the location’s inherent advantages (geography, climate, resource endowments) and the surrounding society’s investments (transport links, institutions, markets). A farm’s productivity, a storefront’s prosperity, or a factory’s site value are all amplified by the public goods that surround them. Yet the current tax system taxes labor, entrepreneurship, and capital while leaving a large portion of land rent untaxed or only lightly taxed. This creates distortions: valuable sites are kept idle or hoarded, urban sprawl is subsidized, and the social surplus produced by location gets captured by private landowners rather than being shared through public services that everyone uses.

Under a 100% unimproved land value tax, the rightful owner—if they own land simply by virtue of location—pays for the privilege of owning that land, not for the improvements they choose to erect on it. Improvements (buildings, drainage, landscaping, infrastructure) are not taxed, or are taxed far less than land values. This distinction is crucial: it prevents double taxation on productive work and capital while ensuring that the passive, value-added payoff that accrues simply from being in a location with public benefits becomes the public’s revenue source. The fairness here is clear: those who benefit from community-created value contribute to sustaining it, while those who improve land or develop it do not bear punitive taxes simply because they chose to use the property in a productive way.

Fairness and justice: removing unearned windfalls from land ownership

Henry George’s central moral intuition—the “unearned windfall” argument—remains the strongest ethical case for a land value tax. Landowners do not create the land’s value by their effort; they do not bear the costs of community growth or public investment that make a place desirable. In a world where valuable land is often monopolized by a few, it is neither just nor efficient to tax productive labor and capital to subsidize a rent that arises from location alone. A 100% unimproved land value tax makes the public’s claim explicit: the community’s collective wealth, created by everyone’s contributions and sacrifices, belongs first to the community itself. If landowners benefit from existing public investment and the social infrastructure that concentrated activity in a given spot, then public revenue should be captured from the resource whose value is derived from that collective contribution.

Moreover, a fully implemented land value tax reduces inequities that arise from geography and historical accident. When public revenue is tied directly to land values, neighborhoods that benefit from proximity to transit, schools, or cultural amenities contribute more to the upkeep of those amenities. This is not a punitive redistribution; it is a fair rent–to–public-benefit mechanism that acknowledges the social dividend baked into the landscape.

Efficiency: tax design that minimizes distortion and aligns incentives

One of the strongest arguments for a land value tax is its unparalleled efficiency. Taxing unimproved land value is essentially non-distortive with respect to productive economic decisions. The tax does not penalize work, investment in improvements, entrepreneurship, or capital formation. If you own land and it’s valuable because of its location, you pay a tax that reflects that value; if you decide to build, you aren’t taxed for the act of improving except insofar as the improvements raise the land’s value (and the unimproved component continues to capture the majority of rent). In practice, this fosters efficient land use in several ways:

  • Preventing land hoarding and speculative stagnation. A 100% LVT reduces the incentive to hold land idle solely for price appreciation, because the tax drives down the land’s unconstrained value over time when it sits unused. This encourages developers to put land into productive use rather than letting it sit fallow while waiting for capital gains to accumulate.

  • Encouraging density and transit-oriented development. Because the tax is on unimproved value, the presence of public infrastructure (subways, buses, street grids, parks) becomes a public asset that supports a higher tax base without punishing efficient, compact, high-value development. The result is smarter, more sustainable urban form and more efficient land markets.

  • Reducing reliance on distortive taxes on labor and capital. When the state’s revenue base comes primarily from land values, the economy experiences less drag on hiring, investment, and entrepreneurship. People can work harder, invest more, and innovate without facing punitive taxes on their productive inputs.

  • Stabilizing public finance over time. Land values tend to track population, infrastructure, and long-run economic growth, providing a relatively stable revenue stream compared to taxes on incomes or profits that can be more volatile. A 100% LVT anchors fiscal policy to a resource that naturally expands with community wealth.

Sole source of government revenue: a cohesive, transparent fiscal system

The Georgist argument for making a land value tax the sole source of government revenue rests on the logic that all other taxes distort behavior and create deadweight loss. Income taxes, payroll taxes, capital gains taxes, sales taxes, and property taxes on improvements all influence decisions in ways that reduce economic efficiency. They also perpetuate revenue instability because they are reactive to business cycles, wage fluctuations, and entrepreneurial risk. If we could design a system in which the public purse is funded entirely by an unimproved land value tax, we would have a transparent, predictable, and fair revenue mechanism aligned with social welfare.

Under this framework:

  • Public revenue would be tied to the value created by the community, not by individuals’ choices about labor or savings. This makes the public sector a partner in the success generated by location and public goods, rather than a punitive extractor of personal effort.

  • Economic incentives would be oriented toward productive investment and efficient land use rather than tax-minimization strategies that exploit loopholes or shift tax burdens across sectors. Landowners would compete for the most productive uses of land, not for ways to minimize tax burdens.

  • Redistributions of wealth would occur through public investment decisions financed by land rents (infrastructure, education, public safety, environmental stewardship, and social services) rather than through complex income redistribution schemes. The social dividend comes from a clearly defined public fund, generated by location-based value rather than by productivity-based taxation.

  • Accountability would be straightforward. If land values rise due to public investment, the tax base grows and the public gains. At the bottom lie taxes on labor and capital (income, corporate, payroll), which create deadweight loss—they discourage the very activities (work, investment, hiring) that generate prosperity. At the top sits the Land Value Tax. A 100% LVT on unimproved value is unique in economic theory: it has zero deadweight loss.

1. Perfect Inelasticity of Supply. Land (unimproved) has a fixed supply. Its supply curve is perfectly vertical. A tax on the value of this fixed supply cannot reduce the quantity supplied. The land does not disappear, flee to a tax haven, or go on strike. The incidence of the tax falls entirely on the landowner, not the tenant. The landlord cannot "pass on" the tax because they are already charging the maximum rent the market will bear. The tax simply separates the publicly created rental value from the privately pocketed price.

2. Elimination of Speculation and Land Hoarding. Under the current system, holding vacant or underutilized land in a booming city is a winning lottery ticket. The speculator contributes nothing, waits for the community to build value around them, and cashes out. A 100% LVT makes holding idle land a liability, not an asset. The annual carrying cost equals the full rental value. This forces land into its highest and best use immediately. Parking lots in downtown cores become housing; abandoned lots become parks or factories; sprawl reverses as infill development becomes profitable. The LVT solves the housing crisis not by subsidizing demand, but by liberating supply.

3. Capital Deepening and Wage Maximization. When taxes on capital (machinery, buildings, inventory, R&D) are abolished, the after-tax return on capital formation skyrockets. Investment floods into productive capacity. Labor becomes relatively scarcer compared to capital, driving wages up to their full marginal product. George’s "Law of Wages" dictates that wages are determined by the margin of production—the return labor can get on free land. By forcing land into use and eliminating the "toll" of private rent, the LVT pushes the margin of production outward, raising the baseline wage for every worker in the economy.

III. The "Single Tax" Necessity: Why Partial Measures Fail

Critics often concede the theoretical elegance of LVT but propose it as a supplement to existing taxes. This is a fatal strategic error. The Single Tax—the 100% LVT as the sole revenue source—is a structural necessity for three reasons.

1. The Fiscal Anchor Prevents Backsliding. As long as the state retains the power to tax income or sales, the political economy remains captured by the landed interest. Landed elites will always lobby to shift the burden onto labor and capital. Only by constitutionally prohibiting all other taxes do we align the state’s revenue interest perfectly with the public good. The state only gets paid when the community thrives and land values rise. The incentives of the treasury and the citizen become identical.

2. Administrative Simplicity and Transparency. Land cannot be hidden in a Swiss bank account, buried in a blockchain, or obscured by creative accounting. It sits there, visible, measurable, and immutable. Assessment requires only a cadaster and market data (comparable sales, income capitalization). The compliance cost approaches zero. The "tax gap" vanishes. The IRS, with its armies of auditors and invasive surveillance of private transactions, becomes obsolete.

3. The Moral Clarity of the Social Contract. A mixed tax system implies a confused social contract: "We own a piece of your labor, a piece of your trade, and a piece of your land." The Single Tax declares a clear, principled compact: "What you create is yours; what the community creates belongs to the community." This clarity is the bedrock of a free society. It ends the class war between labor and capital by revealing their true common opponent: the rentier.

IV. Answering the Objections

“It will destroy small landowners/farmers.” False. The tax is on unimproved value. Agricultural land has low unimproved value per acre. The family farmer, whose wealth is in his improvements (barns, irrigation, soil capital) and his labor, pays little. The corporate agribusiness holding prime suburban land for future development pays the full freight. Furthermore, the abolition of income, payroll, and property taxes on improvements drastically lowers the farmer’s overhead.

“Valuation is impossible.” False. We do it every day for mortgages, insurance, and eminent domain. Modern GIS, hedonic regression models, and transparent auction mechanisms (e.g., "self-assessment with compulsory sale" mechanisms) can determine unimproved value with high accuracy. The residual method (Total Value minus Replacement Cost of Improvements = Land Value) is standard appraisal practice.

“It’s confiscation.” Confiscation is taking what a man made. The 100% LVT takes what the community made. The titleholder retains full possession, full control, and full security of tenure. They simply pay the market rent to the true landlord—the public. If they cannot or will not pay, the land passes to someone who will use it productively. This is not confiscation; it is eviction of the free-rider.

“Capital will flee.” Capital flees taxes on capital. The LVT regime is a capital paradise. Zero corporate tax, zero capital gains tax, zero dividend tax, zero property tax on buildings. The only "cost" is the ground rent—which is a cost that exists regardless of the tax system, currently just pocketed privately. Under LVT, that rent funds public goods that increase land value (infrastructure, safety, education), creating a virtuous cycle.

V. Conclusion: The Birthright of Humanity

The 100% Land Value Tax is not a radical experiment; it is the correction of a primordial error. It aligns the moral law (Thou Shalt Not Steal) with the economic law (Incentives Matter). It transforms the state from a predator on productivity into a dividend-paying cooperative for the shareholders of civilization—the citizens.

By capturing the full rental value of the earth, we socialize the common wealth while rigorously privatizing the individual wealth. We unshackle the builder, the worker, the inventor, and the entrepreneur. We turn the "dead hand" of landed monopoly into the living engine of public revenue.

The choice before us is stark: Do we tax the sweat of the brow, or the value of the ground? Do we penalize the creation of housing, or the hoarding of locations? Do we fund government by punishing virtue, or by collecting the rent of justice?

Henry George offered us the answer: "The tax upon land values is the most just and equal of all taxes... It falls upon those who receive from society a peculiar and valuable benefit, and upon them in proportion to the benefit they receive."

To implement the 100% LVT as the Single Tax is to finally build a civilization where labor receives its full reward, capital its natural return, and the community its rightful rent. It is the economic declaration of independence for the human race. The time for half-measures is over. The land belongs to the living; let them pay its rent to themselves.

Title: The Single Tax: A Moral and Economic Imperative for the 21st Century

In the complex machinery of modern economics, few proposals possess the elegant simplicity and transformative potential of the Land Value Tax (LVT). Championed by the 19th-century political economist Henry George, the concept is radical only in its fairness: a 100% tax on the annual rental value of unimproved land. While contemporary policymakers struggle with labyrinthine tax codes that stifle growth and exacerbate inequality, the Georgist solution offers a clear path forward. Implementing a 100% LVT to replace all other forms of taxation is not merely a fiscal adjustment; it is a moral imperative that aligns the mechanisms of government with the principles of justice, economic efficiency, and the inherent rights of the community.

To understand the necessity of a full LVT, one must first understand the distinction between land and capital. Capital is the product of human labor: the skyscraper, the factory, the tilled field. Land, conversely, is the fixed surface of the earth, a creation of nature, not of man. The value of a specific parcel of land is derived entirely from the community surrounding it. A plot in downtown Tokyo is worth millions not because of the soil quality, but because of the proximity to transit, commerce, and social infrastructure created by the collective effort of society. Therefore, when a private landowner profits from the rise in ground rent—a rise they did not labor to create—they are appropriating the wealth generated by the community. This is the "unearned increment," a privatization of social wealth.

The argument for a 100% LVT is rooted primarily in this conception of justice. Under the current system, a landowner can sit idle on a prime lot in a bustling city, contributing nothing to the economy, yet watch the value of their asset soar due to the industry of their neighbors. This is nothing less than state-sanctioned theft from the commons. By implementing a 100% tax on this unimproved value, society merely reclaims what it created. The tax does not penalize labor or investment; it prevents the monopolization of nature. As George famously argued, we must "abolish all taxation save that upon land values." To tax a man's wages is to punish his industry; to tax his land rent is simply to make him pay for the public benefits he enjoys.

Beyond the moral argument, the economic efficiency of a 100% LVT is undeniable. Standard economic theory dictates that taxes on labor (income tax) and capital (corporate tax, sales tax) create "deadweight loss"—they discourage productive activity. An income tax reduces the incentive to work; a sales tax reduces the incentive to trade. In stark contrast, land is in fixed supply. Taxing the rental value of land does not reduce the amount of land available; the supply is perfectly inelastic. Consequently, a 100% LVT produces zero deadweight loss. It is the only tax that does not distort economic behavior but rather enhances it.

Crucially, a full LVT acts as a potent solvent for the blight of land speculation. Under the current regime, investors often hold prime land out of use, waiting for its value to appreciate, driving up prices for everyone else. This results in sprawling, inefficient cities where developers are forced to build further away from city centers, increasing infrastructure costs and environmental degradation. A 100% LVT would impose a holding cost equal to the land's potential. This would force landholders to either develop the land productively or sell it to someone who will. The result would be a dramatic unlocking of inner-city potential, a reduction in urban sprawl, and a natural suppression of housing costs as the speculative premium is eliminated. This is the "free lunch" that George identified—eliminating the private capture of rent forces capital to be used for productive purposes rather than rent-seeking.

Critics often argue that a single tax on land values would be insufficient to fund modern government. However, empirical studies and economic estimates suggest that the rental value of land constitutes a massive, often underestimated portion of national wealth. In dense urban centers, the land value alone often exceeds the value of the improvements upon it. By capturing this ground rent—the value created by public investment in schools, roads, and security—the government would secure a revenue stream that grows in tandem with the prosperity of the society. It creates a virtuous cycle: public investment raises land values; higher land values fund public services.

Some detractors contend that a 100% tax rate effectively confiscates the land, amounting to a violation of property rights. This relies on a misunderstanding of the Georgist definition of ownership. Under this system, one retains absolute ownership of the capital improvements—the buildings and the fruits of one's labor. But the land itself is viewed as a common trust. The 100% LVT functions as a user fee for the exclusive occupation of a portion of the commons. If one wishes to exclude others from a prime location, one must compensate the community for that privilege. It is the fairest form of payment for a service: the service of secure tenure.

Furthermore, the practical hurdles of valuation are often overstated. In the age of big data and advanced geographic information systems, assessing the value of land separate from improvements is more accurate and administrable than ever before. The IRS currently spends billions processing complex income returns; an LVT system would require a fraction of the administrative overhead, as land cannot be hidden in offshore accounts or moved across borders.

In conclusion, the transition to a 100% Land Value Tax as the sole source of government revenue is the only tax policy that can claim to be both non-punitive and socially beneficial. It ends the injustice of the many enriching the few through land monopoly. It liberates labor and capital from the burdens of taxation, unleashing a wave of productive efficiency. It compels the efficient use of the earth’s finite resources, curbing speculation and urban decay. To implement the Single Tax is to affirm a fundamental truth: that the earth is the common heritage of all mankind, and that the benefits of civilization should be shared by the society that creates them.

  • Improvements: Defined as the result of human labor and capital. This includes buildings, drainage, landscaping, and cultivated crops.

Georgists argue that because land is a natural resource, no individual created it. Therefore, the value of the land itself (unimproved value) is created by the community and nature, not by the landowner.

2. Economic Efficiency: Eliminating Deadweight Loss

A primary economic argument for the Single Tax is efficiency. Most taxes—such as income tax or sales tax—are argued to create "deadweight loss." This occurs because taxes on labor discourage working, and taxes on capital discourage investment. They distort market behavior by discouraging productive activity.

Georgists argue that a tax on the unimproved value of land is different because:

  • Inelastic Supply: The supply of land is fixed. You cannot create more of it, nor can you move it or hide it.
  • No Behavioral Distortion: A tax on land does not reduce the supply of land. A 100% land value tax (LVT) does not discourage the owner from using the land productively because the tax is levied regardless of how the land is used.

Therefore, a land value tax is considered "efficient" because it raises revenue without distorting economic behavior or discouraging production.

3. Eliminating Land Speculation

Georgist theory posits that the private ownership of land allows individuals to profit from "economic rent"—income derived from ownership rather than labor. This encourages land speculation, where individuals purchase land and hold it unused, waiting for its value to rise due to community development (e.g., a new subway line or population growth).

By implementing a 100% tax on the potential rental value of the land:

  • Holding Costs: It becomes expensive to hold land idle. The owner must pay the full rental value to the community annually.
  • Forced Development: To pay the tax, the owner must either develop the land productively or sell it to someone who will.
  • Result: This theoretically ends land speculation, brings idle land into productive use, and reduces urban sprawl by incentivizing the development of prime city locations.

4. Moral and Ethical Justifications

Henry George grounded his philosophy in a moral argument regarding the distribution of wealth.

  • The Labor Theory of Property: George adhered to the principle that individuals have a right to the fruits of their own labor. Taxing wages, sales, or buildings is viewed as penalizing productive activity and violating this right.
  • Community Creation of Value: Georgists argue that land values are socially created. For example, a plot of land in a bustling city is valuable because of the community surrounding it—infrastructure, public services, and the density of the population.

Georgists argue that the rental value of land is sufficient to fund all necessary public services. In dense urban areas where land values are high, the revenue generated could theoretically replace all current taxes. This concept relies on the idea that public investment (schools, roads, police) creates land value, which is then captured via the tax to pay for those services, creating a self-funding cycle.

A wage is tied to labor. A profit is tied (in competitive theory) to innovation, risk-taking, and productive investment. But land rent arises because a site is scarce and strategically located. It is payment for permission to access an opportunity that no owner produced.

Buying land is buying the right to collect what others will pay for access—much of which stems from future community growth and public improvements. Land value rises where public services and infrastructure are good—schools, transit, safety, parks, water systems. This is a form of socialized cost and privatized benefit.

With a full LVT, the loop closes:

  • Public investment raises land value.
  • Higher land value yields higher LVT revenue.
  • That revenue funds public investment (or replaces other taxes).

This is not only fair; it is fiscally honest. The community gets paid back for what it creates.

Economists prize taxes that minimize “deadweight loss”—the reduction in productive activity caused by distorted incentives. A land value tax is uniquely efficient because land supply is fixed. You cannot create less land in response to taxation, and you cannot move it offshore.

Income taxes reduce incentives to work and invest. Payroll taxes raise the cost of hiring. Sales taxes discourage trade and fall heavily on lower-income households. Corporate taxes discourage productive investment and can be passed on through lower wages or higher prices.

  • renovation,
  • machinery,
  • business inventory,
  • wages,
  • entrepreneurship,
  • productive saving.

A 100% LVT changes the calculus:

  • Holding land unused becomes costly.
  • The best response is to put land to its most productive use or sell to someone who will.

This pushes cities toward efficient density where it is most valuable and reduces incentives to leapfrog outward into sprawl. The result is more housing where people want to live, shorter commutes, and better use of existing infrastructure.

Land rent is what remains after paying for labor, capital, and normal returns. If a landlord could raise rents simply because taxes rose, they would have raised rents before. What changes with an LVT is not tenants’ willingness to pay but the division of the surplus: less goes to private landowners, more to the public.

In other words, the LVT captures value that would otherwise be taken as rent. It does not create a new wedge that reduces production; it redirects an existing surplus.

  • It cannot disappear.
  • Assessment can focus on location value, using comparable sales, mass appraisal models, and transparent public data.

A well-designed system can reduce compliance costs and avoidance opportunities that plague other taxes.

A partial LVT is good; a full LVT paired with the elimination of other taxes is transformative. Georgists argue that land rent is not merely an option for revenue but the uniquely appropriate base for public finance.

1. Taxing “goods” and “bads”: current systems tax production; LVT taxes privilege

Most existing taxes fall on activities society generally wants more of: work, building, exchange, investment. They also require intrusive reporting and complex enforcement.

Land rent, by contrast, is not a product of individual effort; it is a socially created value attached to scarcity and location. Capturing it is closer to charging for exclusive privilege than taxing productive behavior. If the purpose of taxation is to fund public goods with minimal harm and maximal fairness, land rent is the best candidate.

2. It turns public growth into public revenue rather than private windfalls

Under conventional finance, economic development and population growth raise land values but do not automatically fund the infrastructure and services that growth requires. Governments then chase revenue by taxing incomes, sales, and buildings—often worsening affordability and slowing development.

With a full LVT, growth itself supplies revenue. When a city becomes more prosperous and land becomes more valuable, public revenue rises correspondingly. The tax base is naturally aligned with the benefits of public order and development.

A large share of wealth inequality stems from land ownership and land price appreciation. When land values rise, owners receive windfalls; non-owners face higher housing costs and barriers to entry. This concentrates wealth across generations, not because of superior productivity, but because of earlier access to ownership.

Capturing land rent:

  • prevents private appropriation of socially created appreciation,
  • reduces speculative price escalation,
  • lowers the purchase price of land (since the future rent is taxed away, land’s sale price falls),
  • makes access to housing and business sites less dominated by inherited advantage.

The result is a fairer distribution without punishing productive success.

4. It’s compatible with markets—and makes them work better

A full LVT is not anti-market. It is pro-competition. When land rent is privatized, markets are distorted because land monopoly lets owners extract wealth without producing. This encourages rent-seeking over entrepreneurship.

By socializing land rent and leaving labor and capital untaxed, the system preserves the price mechanism for allocation while eliminating a central source of unearned income. It rewards productive activity and discourages mere holding of scarce opportunities.

Owners would still control use, improvements, and transfer of buildings and businesses. What changes is that the community charges the full market rent for the community-created value. That is closer to paying for a license to exclude others from a commons than to confiscating someone’s labor.

Moreover, if land rent rightfully belongs to all, then privatizing it is the real confiscation—of everyone else’s equal claim.

Objection 2: “It will hurt farmers and small homeowners.”

A well-designed LVT targets unimproved value; remote agricultural land typically has low location value per acre compared to urban land. High taxes primarily fall where land values are high—city centers and high-opportunity areas—precisely where speculative gains are largest.

For homeowners, the crucial point is that under a land-rent-based system, other taxes disappear: no income tax, no sales tax, no taxes on buildings. Many ordinary households would be better off overall, especially those whose wealth is mostly in improvements and labor rather than high-value sites. Transitional protections can also smooth the shift (deferrals for asset-rich, cash-poor households, phased implementation), but the underlying incidence remains: the biggest payers are those who control the most valuable locations.

Objection 3: “Government revenue won’t be enough.”

Georgists argue that land rent—properly understood—can fund the necessary functions of government because it reflects the value of social order, infrastructure, and economic opportunity. Even where full replacement is debated, the principle remains: the more government and society contribute to making locations valuable, the stronger the revenue potential.

And crucially, eliminating deadweight losses from other taxes can expand the economy, raising land values and thus revenue. A land-value-only system can be self-reinforcing: freeing production increases prosperity; prosperity increases location value; location value funds public goods.

Objection 4: “Assessment is too difficult.”

Assessing land values is not trivial, but it is more tractable than policing global income shifting, corporate profit manipulation, and underground cash economies. Modern appraisal methods can estimate unimproved land values using sales data, residual methods (subtracting improvement value), and statistical modeling. Transparency and frequent reassessment reduce corruption and appeals.

The difficulty of assessment is an argument for better administration, not for taxing work and trade instead.

A 100% land value tax embodies a clean social bargain:

  • You keep what you earn and build.
  • You pay society for the value society gives your location.
  • Public services are funded by public-created value, not by penalties on production.

This strengthens both liberty and community. It removes the government’s incentive to intrude into private transactions to measure income, spending, or profits. It also reduces the political temptation to carve the economy into special exemptions and loopholes—because land cannot be moved, hidden, or relabeled as easily as income.

Most importantly, it ends a quiet injustice at the core of modern economies: the treatment of land appreciation as a private reward rather than a collective dividend. When land rent is privatized, the many pay the few for access to opportunity. When land rent is captured publicly, the value of living together is returned to everyone—either through better services, lower barriers to work and enterprise, or direct dividends.

Conclusion: the most defensible tax base is the one no one produces

A 100% tax on the unimproved value of land is not an attack on property; it is a defense of productive property against the rival claim of monopoly. It is fair because it socializes what society creates and leaves individuals what they create. It is efficient because it does not shrink the supply of land or punish labor and capital. It is uniquely capable of curbing speculation, lowering artificial scarcity in housing and business sites, and aligning public revenue with public progress.

If the goal of government revenue is to fund shared needs while respecting individual freedom and maximizing prosperity, then the best—and ultimately the only—legitimate source is the one base that cannot be earned, cannot be hidden, and cannot be justified as a private creation: land rent. Capturing it fully is not merely a policy option. It is the most coherent expression of equal rights, competitive markets, and a society that rewards production rather than privilege.
