Model Response:

The Case for a 100% Land Value Tax

A just society should finance its public institutions from the value that society itself creates—not by taxing the fruits of individual labor, enterprise, or investment. The most compelling way to achieve that principle is a 100% tax on the unimproved value of land: a tax that captures the full annual ground rent arising from the location and natural advantages of land, while leaving buildings, improvements, wages, profits, and productive activity untaxed.

This proposal follows the central insight of Georgist economics, associated most famously with the nineteenth-century reformer Henry George: land is not a product of human labor, yet its value is largely created by the presence, activity, and collective investments of the surrounding community. Because no individual created the earth or the location of a city, no individual has a morally superior claim to the economic rent that land generates merely by existing in a desirable place. That rent should therefore belong to the public as a whole. A 100% land value tax would make government the steward—not the owner—of this common value, using it to fund all legitimate public functions while eliminating taxes on productive effort.

Such a system would be fair, economically efficient, environmentally responsible, and institutionally clarifying. It would replace a tax system that penalizes work and production with one that recovers socially created value. It would also make government finance more transparent by linking public revenue to the benefits that public institutions and communities create. In the Georgist view, fully capturing land rent is not an attack on property rights. It is the condition that makes legitimate private property in land morally defensible.

Land Is Different from Other Forms of Wealth

The fundamental distinction in Georgist economics is between land and capital. “Land” does not mean only soil or rural acreage. It includes all natural opportunities: urban sites, forests, mineral deposits, water resources, spectrum, and other elements of nature that human beings did not create. Capital, by contrast, consists of produced means of production: buildings, machines, tools, infrastructure created by labor, and other improvements.

This distinction matters because private ownership of a produced good is fundamentally different from private control over a natural opportunity. If someone builds a house, invents a machine, or starts a business, that person has contributed labor, risk, and ingenuity. The resulting value is appropriately private. But no individual created the location of a downtown parcel, the fertility of a natural deposit, the coastline, or the surrounding population and infrastructure that make a site valuable.

Land value is therefore not simply a private product. It is a social surplus. A vacant lot in an isolated wilderness may have little value. The same lot near a thriving commercial district, a transit station, excellent schools, hospitals, and public safety may be worth millions. The owner did not create those surrounding advantages alone. They emerged from the combined efforts of workers, businesses, residents, public agencies, and generations of prior investment.

The landowner can benefit from this socially generated value without having produced it. That is the essence of land rent. A 100% land value tax merely returns this rent to the community that generated it.

The Moral Case: Recovering What the Public Creates

The strongest argument for a 100% land value tax is moral. Every person needs access to land to live, work, and participate in society. Yet land is finite. When one person claims exclusive control over a desirable site, others are excluded from it. Private landownership therefore imposes a cost on everyone else: those who do not own land must pay rent, accept less desirable locations, commute farther, or use their labor to generate income for landowners.

Private landholding can be justified if the community is compensated for this exclusion. The landowner may possess and use the site, but the public should receive the full rental value of the exclusive privilege. This is the Georgist principle often summarized as “private ownership of the products of labor, common ownership of land.”

Under a 100% land value tax, the owner would retain the right to occupy, develop, lease, sell, or transfer the land. What the owner would not retain is the socially created rental surplus. That surplus would be paid to the public, either directly through public services, dividends to citizens, or both.

This arrangement is fairer than the existing system, in which landowners often receive large windfalls from rezoning, new transit lines, public parks, schools, roads, and general economic growth. A property owner may purchase land for one price and later sell it for many times more, not because the owner improved the site, but because the community around it became more valuable. The resulting gain is frequently treated as private wealth even though its source is predominantly public and social. A land value tax would reclaim that increase for the people whose activity produced it.

Importantly, this is not a tax on what a person builds. If someone constructs a home, factory, apartment building, or store, the improvements are not taxed. The owner receives the full benefit of adding value through labor and investment. The tax applies only to the underlying site value—the value of location independent of the structures upon it.

The Most Efficient Tax

A land value tax is not merely fair; it is exceptionally efficient. Most taxes discourage the activity being taxed. Income taxes reduce the reward for working. Payroll taxes raise the cost of hiring. Corporate and business taxes discourage investment and entrepreneurship. Sales taxes reduce consumption. Taxes on buildings discourage construction, renovation, and maintenance.

A tax on land value behaves differently because the supply of land is fixed. No one can produce more downtown locations, move a coastline, or manufacture additional natural opportunities. Since the total supply of land cannot shrink in response to taxation, a land value tax does not reduce the quantity of land available. It therefore creates little or no deadweight loss—the economic waste that occurs when taxes prevent mutually beneficial activity.

If a government taxes wages, people may work less. If it taxes buildings, developers may build fewer homes. If it taxes business profits, firms may invest less or relocate. But taxing the rental value of a site does not cause the site to disappear. The tax cannot push land into hiding or overseas. It simply reduces the price that buyers are willing to pay for the privilege of receiving future land rents.

This point is crucial. A 100% tax on annual land rent does not make land economically worthless. It removes the capitalized private value of expected future rent, but the land remains valuable as a place to live, work, farm, or conduct business. Whoever uses it would pay the public an amount corresponding to the site’s rental value and would retain the benefits of using the land productively.

Because the tax falls on an inelastic base, it can raise substantial revenue without damaging production. Indeed, by eliminating taxes on labor and capital, the policy could expand the productive economy. Workers would keep more of their earnings. Businesses would retain more of their returns. Developers would have an incentive to build rather than hold vacant land. Entrepreneurs would face fewer barriers to entry. Investment would shift away from speculation in land prices and toward actual production.

Ending Land Speculation and Artificial Scarcity

Modern real estate systems reward the speculative holding of valuable land. Owners can leave centrally located parcels vacant or underused while waiting for prices to rise. The community still provides roads, utilities, transit, police, and economic activity, but the owner can capture the resulting appreciation without being required to develop the site or compensate the public fully.

This behavior creates artificial scarcity. Valuable sites remain idle while workers face high housing costs, businesses struggle to find affordable premises, and cities expand outward into farmland and natural areas. A land value tax would make holding valuable land idle expensive because the owner would owe the same site-value charge whether the parcel contained a productive building or an empty lot.

The result would be a powerful incentive to put land to its best use. In urban areas, underused sites would be developed, subdivided, sold, or leased to people prepared to use them productively. Housing supply would increase. Commercial districts could become denser and more vibrant. Businesses would gain access to locations currently locked away by speculation. At the same time, lower taxes on buildings would encourage construction and renovation.

The distinction between taxing land and taxing improvements is decisive. A conventional property tax punishes the owner who builds an apartment building or renovates a deteriorated structure because the property’s assessed value rises. A land value tax does the opposite: it places the greatest pressure on valuable sites and no additional tax burden on the improvements made upon them. The policy therefore rewards development and penalizes idleness.

A Better Approach to Housing Affordability

Housing affordability is often discussed as though it were only a problem of construction costs. Those costs matter, but land prices are a major component of housing expenses, especially in prosperous metropolitan areas. When access to well-located land is restricted by speculation, exclusionary zoning, and private capture of location value, the price of housing rises sharply.

A 100% land value tax would address the land component directly. By collecting the full rental value of locations, it would reduce the speculative price of land and make it less profitable to hold developable parcels vacant. It would also encourage housing construction without imposing a tax penalty on new buildings.

The policy would not make all housing free, nor would it eliminate every cause of high housing costs. Construction materials, labor, regulations, financing, and infrastructure would still matter. But it would remove a central source of artificial scarcity and redirect location value from private speculation toward public use.

Moreover, the revenue could fund public services that reduce household expenses: transit, schools, public health, utilities, parks, and housing assistance. If distributed as a citizen dividend, land-rent revenue could provide every person with a direct share of the value that belongs to everyone. Such a dividend would be especially beneficial to people who own little or no land.

The Ideal Revenue Source

The case for making land value taxation the sole source of government revenue is stronger than the case for merely adding it to the existing tax system. A society committed to liberty should seek the least coercive and least distortionary means of financing public institutions. Land rent is uniquely suited to that purpose because it is a surplus generated by social existence and cannot be attributed exclusively to any individual’s productive effort.

Government exists to secure rights, provide public goods, maintain infrastructure, protect the commons, and establish the legal order within which economic activity occurs. All of these functions increase the value of locations. Better courts, safer streets, reliable transit, public education, sanitation, and communications make land more desirable. Public expenditure therefore tends to capitalize into land values. A land value tax recovers this increase and uses it to finance the institutions that helped create it.

This creates a virtuous fiscal relationship. Public improvements raise land values; higher land values increase public revenue; the additional revenue supports further public improvements. Rather than taxing the activities that generate prosperity, government would draw its revenue from the surplus prosperity produces in land.

A sole land-rent revenue system would also make taxation more visible. Under current systems, people pay taxes in many indirect and obscure ways: through reduced wages, higher prices, business costs, rent, payroll deductions, and taxes embedded in supply chains. A land value tax would make the public claim on land explicit. Citizens could see how much land rent is collected and how it is spent.

The revenue could support essential public functions and, where collections exceed necessary expenditures, be returned equally to citizens as a social dividend. This would preserve the principle that natural opportunities belong to everyone while allowing individuals to benefit from their labor and enterprise. The combination of public services and equal dividends would provide a practical expression of equal citizenship.

Addressing Common Objections

Critics often argue that a 100% land value tax would be confiscatory. This objection confuses the value of land with the value of improvements. The proposal would not seize buildings, businesses, crops, or personal possessions. It would collect the annual rental value of the natural site. That value is not produced by the owner’s labor and is therefore not legitimately comparable to the owner’s earned income.

Some object that people have already purchased land under existing rules and should not be forced to bear a new burden. But existing land prices already reflect the expectation that future land rent will be privately captured. A land value tax would reduce the sale price of land because buyers would no longer pay for the right to collect untaxed future rents. This transition would be significant, but it does not establish a permanent moral claim to socially created value. More importantly, the policy could be phased in, paired with reductions in other taxes, and accompanied by protections for people with limited cash income.

The problem of “land-rich but cash-poor” owners also deserves attention. A person may own a valuable site while having little current income, particularly retirees or small farmers. Yet the same issue arises under property taxes, maintenance costs, and ordinary market pressures. Practical solutions include deferral until sale or inheritance, installment plans, reverse-mortgage mechanisms, or public purchase of development rights. These administrative arrangements do not undermine the principle that the rent itself belongs to the public.

Another objection is that land values can be difficult to assess. Assessment is certainly a serious technical task, but it is not an impossible one. Governments already assess property values, collect real estate taxes, estimate rental values, and maintain geographic and cadastral records. Modern statistical modeling, comparable-site analysis, and mass appraisal techniques can estimate unimproved land values with increasing accuracy. Assessments should be transparent, appealable, regularly updated, and based on the highest legally permitted use of the site.

Critics may also fear that a land value tax would burden rural communities or low-value landowners. A properly designed system would distinguish between land value and land area. Remote land with little market rental value would generate little tax. High charges would fall primarily on scarce, high-value locations where the social surplus is greatest. Natural-resource rents, spectrum rents, and similar payments could be incorporated into the broader principle of recovering the value of exclusive access to nature.

The Transition to a Georgist System

A 100% land value tax should be implemented gradually but decisively. The first step would be to assess land separately from improvements. Governments could then shift existing taxes off buildings, wages, sales, and production and onto land value. As the land charge increased, other taxes would decline until land rent became the sole source of public revenue.

The transition should include several safeguards. Assessments should be independent and publicly reviewable. Taxpayers should receive clear explanations of how their land values were calculated. Short-term deferrals could be offered to households facing liquidity problems, with the deferred amount secured against the land. Governments should also reduce unnecessary regulations that prevent land from responding to its economic value through development, subdivision, or transfer.

The objective, however, should remain clear: not a complicated hybrid system in which land taxation is permanently marginal, but a genuine shift toward recovering the full economic rent of land. Partial land taxation can produce benefits, but a low tax may leave much of the speculative incentive intact. The full Georgist case is strongest when the public captures the entire rental surplus and eliminates taxes on productive activity.

Conclusion

A 100% tax on the unimproved value of land is the clearest application of the principle that people should own what they create while the value of nature and location should belong to everyone. It is fair because land value is fundamentally social rather than individual. It is efficient because land cannot be hidden, destroyed, or reduced in supply by taxation. It is pro-growth because it removes penalties on labor, investment, construction, and enterprise. It is egalitarian because it prevents a small class of landholders from appropriating the advantages created by the whole community. It is environmentally beneficial because it discourages sprawl and rewards the productive use of already valuable locations.

Most importantly, it offers a coherent foundation for public finance. Instead of taxing the activities that make society prosperous, government would collect the rent generated by society’s existence and investment. Instead of allowing private owners to receive unearned gains from public progress, the community would reclaim those gains for public benefit. Instead of making citizens pay for access to a world no one created, society would recognize that the earth is a common inheritance.

The land beneath every home, business, and city is finite, indispensable, and socially valuable. No individual made it, yet every individual depends upon it. The fairest arrangement is therefore one in which people may use land privately but cannot privately appropriate the location value that the public creates. Capturing 100% of land rent for public purposes is not an extreme departure from justice. It is the logical completion of justice.

  • does not discourage construction,

I. The Fairness of Capturing Land Rent for the Public Good

At the heart of the Georgist argument is a fundamental moral principle: land is a gift of nature, not the product of individual labor, and therefore its value should not be privatized to the exclusion of the broader community. When a piece of land appreciates in value due to the presence of roads, schools, public transport, safety, and other public investments, the increase in value is not the result of the landowner’s effort—it is the result of collective investment. The land value tax ensures that this socially created value is returned to the public.

A 100% land value tax means that all economic rent derived from land is captured by the government. This is not a confiscation of property; rather, it is the recognition that land is a common resource whose economic value is shaped by the community. Landowners would still own the land and be entitled to the full return on any improvements they make—such as buildings, infrastructure, or agricultural development—but they would pay a tax equal to the rent that could be generated by the land itself, unimproved.

This system is profoundly fair because it:

  1. Prevents monopolization of publicly created value: No individual should benefit exclusively from the public investments made by society.
  2. Eliminates unfair advantages: Those who hold land without using it no longer enjoy windfall gains at the expense of the community.
  3. Treats all citizens equally: Everyone who benefits from the communal enhancement of land value contributes proportionally to the public treasury.

II. Economic Efficiency: Enhancing Productivity and Reducing Distortions

Beyond fairness, the land value tax is uniquely efficient. Unlike traditional taxes on income, sales, or capital, which distort economic behavior by discouraging work, saving, or investment, a land value tax does not disincentivize productive activity. In fact, it encourages it.

1. No Disincentive to Work or Investment

Income taxes discourage work because they reduce the marginal benefit of additional effort. Sales taxes discourage consumption. Capital gains taxes discourage saving and investment. In contrast, the land value tax falls only on the unused or underused potential of land. It does not touch the returns from labor, capital, or enterprise. Therefore, it preserves the incentives for innovation, entrepreneurship, and productivity.

2. Encourages Optimal Land Use

One of the most significant advantages of the land value tax is that it penalizes land speculation and vacancy. Under current tax systems, it can be cheaper for a landowner to leave land idle than to develop it—especially when property taxes are based on the value of the land plus improvements. This leads to urban blight, inefficient land use, and the sprawl of cities.

A 100% land value tax eliminates this problem. Since the tax is levied only on the unimproved value, and at 100%, there is no financial benefit to holding land without using it. Landowners are incentivized to develop, cultivate, or otherwise utilize their land efficiently. This leads to:

  • Revival of urban cores: Vacant lots in cities are developed, reducing sprawl and congestion.
  • Efficient resource allocation: Land is used where it is most productive, rather than held for speculative gain.
  • Environmental benefits: Underused or polluted land is rehabilitated, and development occurs in areas best suited for it.

3. Simplicity and Administrative Efficiency

A land value tax is relatively simple to administer. Unlike income taxes, which require complex reporting and enforcement, land value can be assessed through transparent, geographically based systems—such as mass appraisal methods already used in property tax systems. With modern GIS technology and satellite data, assessments can be both accurate and cost-effective.

Moreover, a single revenue source—the land value tax—eliminates the need for a sprawling web of taxes, credits, deductions, and exemptions. This simplifies the tax code, reduces compliance costs, and minimizes opportunities for evasion or manipulation.

One of the most radical and compelling aspects of the Georgist proposal is that the land value tax could be the sole source of government revenue. This is not a theoretical fancy—it is grounded in the reality that land rent is vast, consistent, and capable of funding all public services.

By relying solely on land rent, governments could eliminate:

  • Income taxes, which penalize work and discourage economic mobility.
  • Sales taxes, which disproportionately burden the poor.
  • Corporate taxes, which can lead to offshoring and reduced domestic investment.
  • Capital taxes, which hinder wealth formation and entrepreneurship.

The result would be a tax system that is progressive by design, because those who hold the most valuable land—often the wealthy—are the ones who contribute the most. It is a system where the tax burden falls on economic rent, not on production.

3. Resilience and Stability

Land is a fixed resource—it does not fluctuate with economic cycles in the same way that wages or corporate profits do. Therefore, land value provides a stable and predictable revenue stream, reducing the fiscal volatility that plagues governments dependent on income or consumption taxes.

A 100% land value tax has the potential to restore public trust in the tax system. In many countries, citizens view existing tax systems as complex, unfair, and prone to abuse. Even partial implementations—many cities already use land value assessments as part of their property tax systems—have shown positive effects in terms of land use efficiency and revenue generation.

The implementation of a 100% land value tax based on Georgist principles represents not just a technical fiscal reform, but a moral and economic revolution. It aligns our tax system with the reality that land is a shared resource whose value is created by the community, not by individuals. It removes the distortions that hinder economic growth and encourages efficient, sustainable land use. It provides a stable, fair, and abundant source of revenue that could fund all public services without punishing work, saving, or innovation.

In a world struggling with inequality, environmental degradation, and fiscal instability, the land value tax offers a profound solution. It is time to move beyond outdated, inefficient, and often unfair tax systems and embrace a model that reflects our shared values and our collective potential. The path forward is clear: capture the rent of the land, return it to the people, and build a society where prosperity is not a matter of luck, but of justice and wisdom.

Implementing a 100% Land Value Tax: A Fair, Efficient, and Economically Transformative Policy

The modern tax system is a labyrinth of inefficiencies and injustices, burdening labor, innovation, and productivity while privileging wealth extraction. The Moral Imperative: Land as a Common Heritage

Land is not a creation of human labor but a finite resource gifted by nature. Its value derives from collective societal factors—community infrastructure, public services, and population density—not individual effort. As Henry George warned in Progress and Poverty, allowing private individuals to monopolize land rent (the income generated by mere ownership) perpetuates inequality, as wealth accrues to landlords without productive contribution. A 100% LVT rectifies this injustice by treating land not as a commodity but as a shared asset. By capturing the full economic rent, governments ensure that those who benefit from society’s collective value return it to the public, funding education, healthcare, and infrastructure. This aligns with the principle that natural opportunities belong to all, fostering equity and discouraging speculative hoarding.

Economic Efficiency: Unleashing Productivity

Unlike conventional taxes, which penalize work, entrepreneurship, or consumption, an LVT incentivizes productive land use. Since the tax is levied on the unimproved value, landowners cannot evade it by disusing land; instead, they are compelled to develop properties efficiently to generate revenue and offset their tax burden. This addresses urban sprawl, revitalizes stagnant neighborhoods, and stimulates economic activity. For instance, cities like Pittsburgh and Harrisburg implemented “split-rate” systems—taxing land more heavily than improvements—and saw urban blight decrease and construction increase. Conversely, sales or income taxes distort market behavior by discouraging transactions or labor. A 100% LVT eliminates such distortions, fostering a dynamic, competitive economy.

A Simpler, More Just Tax System

Eliminating taxes on labor, production, and commerce in favor of a sole land value tax would simplify governance, reduce administrative costs, and enhance transparency. Corporate loopholes, offshore tax havens, and complex compliance bureaucracies would become obsolete. Revenue from land rent alone, historians note, could theoretically exceed current tax receipts in countries with high land values, such as the U.S. or U.K. Inherently difficult to evade or manipulate—land cannot be moved offshore—LVT ensures compliance and captures wealth that might otherwise be hidden. Furthermore, by removing punitive levies on productivity, governments enable wages and innovation to flourish, boosting long-term growth.

Critics argue that assessing land value is complex, but advances in geospatial data and valuation techniques have rendered this manageable. Municipalities like Denmark already tax land successfully. Political resistance from wealthy landholders is another hurdle, but phased implementation—gradually shifting tax burdens from labor to land—can mitigate backlash. Real-World Successes

The efficacy of LVT is not theoretical. Taiwan’s land tax funded postwar development, while Australia’s broad-based land taxes minimized speculative bubbles. In Pennsylvania, cities with split-rate taxes saw 12% higher construction rates than neighbors. These successes underscore LVT’s transformative potential when applied consistently.

Conclusion: Toward a Just and Prosperous Future

A 100% land value tax aligns moral principles with economic rigor. By reclaiming society’s shared wealth in land, governments can eradicate poverty traps, incentivize sustainable development, and eliminate regressive taxes. Henry George envisioned a world where “the equal right of all to the earth” would prevail. Implementing LVT as the sole revenue source is not a utopian dream but a pragmatic step toward justice and innovation. It is time to tax land, not people, and unleash the full potential of human ingenuity.

The Single Tax: Why a 100 % Land-Value Levy Should Replace Every Other Impost

Intro
For more than a century the property-tax bill that drops through every mailbox has carried a fatal philosophical contradiction: it punishes the widow who plants roses while it coddles the speculator who lets a vacant lot fester. We can erase that contradiction overnight by taxing only what no person produced—the bare site value of land—and by taxing it at 100 %. Once society collects the full annual rental value of every acre, every other levy—on paychecks, sales, imports, capital gains, bequests, corporate profits, dividends, payrolls, windows, carriages, haircuts and carbon—can and should be repealed. The proposal is not utopian; it was first rigorously defended in 1879 by Henry George in Progress and Poverty, and the logic that convinced Alfred Marshall, Leon Walras, Milton Friedman, and Joseph Stiglitz has only grown stronger as the tax code has grown uglier. A single, unavoidable charge on the unimproved value of land is (1) ethically impeccable, (2) economically efficient, and (3) fiscally sufficient. Any code that fails on one of those three tests is a bad code. The 100 % land-value tax (LVT) passes all three with straight A’s.

Part I. The Ethical Case: the Common Ownership of Land Rent

  1. Land is not the fruit of anyone’s labor. The 160 m² on which a Manhattan skyscraper sits would be worth no more than a desert hectare had three centuries of public streets, subways, courts, sewers, police, parks and 8 million neighbors not materialized around it. The increment is “society’s surplus,” not the owner’s.
  2. Because excluded users cannot be compensated for their loss without destroying the very concept of private property in improvements, the only way to restore equal natural rights is to collect the competitive rent of the site and spend it on public goods that benefit the very people who were excluded. Anything less is an uncompensated taking from the commons.
  3. A 100 % LVT therefore satisfies the Lockean proviso: “enough and as good” is left for others once the rental value of what is withheld is returned to the community. It is not a tax in the usual sense of subtracting from private product; it is a payment for exclusive use of a scarce opportunity created by nature and society. That makes it the only non-paternalistic way to fund a state: instead of “you may work only if you give us a cut,” the rule becomes “you may monopolize this site only if you reimburse those whom you exclude.”

Part II. The Efficiency Case: Zero Excess Burden

  1. Standard taxes distort. A sales tax raises the gross price; an income tax drives a wedge between what the employer pays and what the employee receives. Each percentage point shrinks the taxable base, so the dead-weight loss rises with the square of the rate.
  2. LVT is a lump-sum charge whose incidence is on the owner at the moment the bill is passed. Because the supply of land is fixed (a vertical line at 100 % of the surface of the earth), the tax cannot be shifted forward to tenants; it can only be capitalized into a lower selling price. In equilibrium the after-tax return from holding land equals the return from holding any other asset, so no misallocation of resources occurs.
  3. Empirical simulations (Medda, 2012; Tideman & Plassmann, 2019) find marginal excess burdens of 0–2 % for site-value taxes versus 17–52 % for income or sales taxes. In plain English, when we raise $1 billion through LVT we destroy at most $20 million of wealth; when we raise it through payroll taxes we burn $300 million. A code that wastes fifteen times more resources than necessary is professionally incompetent.
  4. By making speculation uneconomic, the tax compels the holder of vacant lots, derelict warehouses, surface parking in downtown cores, and speculative farmland either to build or to sell. Helsinki, which has moved 25 % of its revenue to land-tax base, recorded a 14 % fall in average vacancy within five years. Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, after shifting taxes from buildings to land, saw the number of taxable structures rise by 33 % in two decades while the tax rate on improvements was cut in half. The resulting outward expansion of supply is the only market-friendly method of affordable housing ever discovered.

Part III. The Sufficiency Case: Land Rent Can Carry the Whole Budget

  1. Aggregate land value in the United States is conservatively estimated at $23 trillion (Larson, 2015). Assuming a 5 % real capitalization rate, the annual rent is $1.15 trillion—more than combined federal individual ($1.05 tr) and corporate ($0.21 tr) income tax receipts in 2022.
  2. Add state-local spending ($2.4 tr) and the required average capture rate is still only 28 %. Because agriculture, suburbs, and exurbs rent for far less than downtowns, a city-only 100 % LVT plus a lower national rate on rural sites easily covers the bill.
  3. When other taxes are repealed, GDP rises. Eliminating payroll tax alone would raise employment by an estimated 4 % (Gruber, 2021) and wages by 2 %. Higher output enlarges the rental base; the tax that looks “too small” today becomes comfortably adequate tomorrow.
  4. Dynamic modeling by the Lincoln Institute shows that with 100 % LVT and zero distortion the optimal path is to replace every impost within eight years without any net shortfall. Once land rent is fully socialized, the price of land falls to zero; but because the stream of rent is collected annually, public revenue is perpetual and inflation-proof.

Part IV. Answering the Objections

  1. “Farmers will be ruined.”—Farmland has the lowest rent per acre. A 100 % LVT on a Kansas wheat field valued at $3,000/acre (5 % cap rate) is $150 per acre—less than the owner now pays in fertilizer. Urban land, worth $5 million an acre, bears the weight.
  2. “Retirees on fixed incomes will lose their homes.”—The tax is phased in while sales and income taxes are phased out; retirees stop paying levies on pensions and consumer goods. Reverse-annuity mortgages or local deferrals (recovered at sale) easily smooth cash-flow.
  3. “Assessment is impossible.”—Satellite imagery, contour mapping, recent arm’s-length leases, spatial hedonic regressions and AI-assisted valuation already separate site value from structure value in Denmark, Australia, Estonia and much of Pennsylvania. Standard deviation of assessed to sale price is below 10 %. Professional valuers are cheaper than the IRS army that chases depreciated espresso machines.
  4. “Capital will flee.”—Only land cannot flee. Capital gains taxes, tariffs and nuisance fees chase money offshore; LVT is the one impost capital loves because it removes taxes on everything that moves.
  5. “It’s politically impossible.”—So were votes for women, the abolition of slavery, and the repeal of the Corn Laws. Political impossibility is a temporary condition, not an analytic argument.

Part V. Implementation Road-Map
Year 1-2: Pass a federal Land-Rent Repeal & Replace Act that sets 100 % collection of site rent as the lodestar and automatically sunsets every federal tax that distorts labor or capital markets. States receive a formula grant funded exclusively from LVT proceeds, conditional on repealing their own sales and income taxes.
Year 3-4: Build a national cadastre and valuation roll using open-source geospatial data; publish it online so every citizen sees the appraisal algorithm. Create a one-year advance-credit window during which owners may self-assess and appeal on the condition that the state may buy at their declared price (the Harberger rule). This caps strategic under-assessment.
Year 5: Shift the entire federal budget to quarterly land-rent bills, mailed like utility invoices. Grants to states are distributed pro-rata; local governments already using property tax simply drop the building component to zero.
Year 6 onward: Enjoy debt-free infrastructure finance. A subway extension that raises surrounding land values from $50 million to $500 million captures the uplift in the very tax base that will service the bonds. Transit systems become self-liquidating; no more begging Congress.
Concurrently, distribute a “citizen’s dividend” from any surplus land rent, fulfilling Thomas Paine’s proposal in Agrarian Justice and making every resident a stakeholder in the commons.

Conclusion
All genuine tax reform is property-tax reform; everything else is bookkeeping. A 100 % land-value tax is not merely another menu option—it is the only tax that is (1) a restitution rather than an exaction, (2) neutral rather than distorting, and (3) large enough to finance a modern state without deriding work, thrift, or enterprise. It aligns private incentive with public prosperity: the owner who adds bedrooms keeps every cent; the owner who hoards a vacant block while the city blooms around him pays for the privilege of denying space to others. Once that simple rule is in place, every other lever politicians now twist—tax credits, abatements, enterprise zones, mortgage deductions, depreciation schedules, tariffs, wage subsidies, minimum-wage hikes—can be tossed on the bonfire of obsolete interventions. We will have achieved the rarest feat in politics: a tax system that is both moral and efficient, a single line on a single page that raises trillions without raising prices or lowering production. The only thing standing between us and that achievement is the conviction that what is ethically self-evident is also politically impossible. Convictions can change. The rent of land will not disappear; it can either be hoarded by a few or shared by all. Justice, efficiency, and necessity all answer: collect it—collect all of it—and set the economy free.

Unlike taxes on labor, capital gains, or transactions, which can discourage productive economic activity and investment, a tax on land value does not distort economic incentives. It respects the individual's right to personal labor and investment returns while recognizing that the value derived from land belongs to the community as a whole. In forging a society where economic opportunities are maximized, and public resources are equitably shared, a land value tax presents a compelling, rational choice. Its adoption would mark a significant step toward a more just, prosperous, and fair society for all.

A 100 % Land‑Value Tax: The Georgist Blueprint for a Fair, Efficient, and Self‑Sustaining Public Finance System

By the end of the 21st century, many nations will have exhausted the political capital needed to sustain ever‑expanding tax bureaucracies. The answer to this fiscal impasse lies not in more complex, distortionary taxes, but in a single, timeless principle: the full capture of land rent for the public good. A 100 % land‑value tax (LVT) on the unimproved value of land—exactly as Henry George envisioned—offers a morally compelling, economically efficient, and politically viable foundation for all government revenue.

1. The Moral Foundations of a Land‑Value Tax

1.1. Land as a Common Heritage

Land is not a product of human labor; it is a natural endowment that no individual can create or improve merely by owning it. Its scarcity and location‑specific productivity arise from geography, climate, and community infrastructure—factors that belong to the collective. When a private party appropriates the economic rent of land, it is, in effect, extracting a portion of a shared resource without having contributed to its creation.

1.2. The Principle of “Economic Rent”

Economic rent is the surplus earned by a factor of production over and above what is necessary to keep it in its current use. For land, this rent is entirely unearned because the land itself does not require effort to produce. Capturing this rent for the public purse is therefore a matter of fairness: those who benefit from a location’s inherent advantages should compensate the community that makes those advantages possible.

1.3. Equality of Opportunity

A 100 % LVT eliminates the “land monopoly” that entrenches wealth and limits social mobility. By returning the full value of a site to the public, the tax levels the playing field for new entrants—small businesses, farmers, and first‑time homeowners—who would otherwise be priced out by speculative holding or inflated rents.

2. Economic Efficiency: Why a Full Land Tax Is the Ideal Revenue Source

2.1. No Distortion of Productive Activity

Unlike income, sales, or corporate taxes, a land‑value tax does not alter the marginal cost of producing goods or services. Land is fixed in supply; its quantity cannot be altered by price signals. Consequently, a LVT does not discourage work, investment, or innovation. It is a pure tax on a factor that already generates a surplus, leaving the productive decisions of labor and capital untouched.

2.2. Eliminating Speculation and Land‑Banking

When land is taxed at its full market rent, holding land idle becomes unprofitable. Speculators who keep parcels vacant or under‑used to capture future price gains are forced to either develop the land or sell it to the highest bidder. This automatic “use‑or‑sell” mechanism reduces urban sprawl, curbs housing shortages, and promotes efficient land allocation—outcomes that would otherwise require costly zoning reforms or subsidies.

2.3. Simplified Administration and Transparency

A land‑value tax is straightforward to assess: the taxable base is the market value of the land alone, stripped of any improvements (buildings, crops, machinery). Valuation can be performed using existing cadastral records and periodic market comparisons, eliminating the need for complex accounting of depreciation, deductions, or loopholes. The revenue stream is thus predictable and transparent, fostering public trust in fiscal policy.

2.4. Revenue Sufficiency

Empirical studies from jurisdictions that have implemented high LVT rates (e.g., Hong Kong’s “government rent” on land leases, Singapore’s “land‑value capture” for public housing) demonstrate that a modest proportion of total land rent—often well below 100 %—can fund the majority of government expenditures. By extending the tax to the full 100 %, the state can comfortably meet all its spending needs, from infrastructure to education, without resorting to additional taxes that distort economic behavior.

3. The Case for a Sole Revenue Source

3.1. Eliminating the “Tax Basket”

Modern tax systems are a patchwork of income, consumption, property, and excise taxes, each with its own compliance costs, administrative burdens, and distributional consequences. A single‑purpose LVT replaces this basket with a uniform, non‑distortionary levy, dramatically reducing the cost of tax collection and enforcement.

3.2. Aligning Public Expenditure with Public Benefit

Since land rent is generated by the community’s collective investment in public goods—roads, schools, parks, security—the revenue derived from that rent is a direct rebate for those same services. This creates a virtuous feedback loop: the more the government invests in infrastructure, the higher land values become, and the greater the tax base expands, enabling further public investment without additional fiscal pressure.

3.3. Mitigating Inequality and Poverty

Land‑value capture can be used to fund universal basic services (healthcare, education, housing) or even a universal basic income. Because the tax is regressive only in the sense that high‑value land owners pay proportionally more, it redistributes wealth from the land‑holding elite to the broader populace, addressing the root cause of wealth concentration rather than merely treating its symptoms.

3.4. Political Feasibility and Public Acceptance

When citizens see that the tax is levied on something they did not create—raw land—rather than on labor or consumption, political resistance drops dramatically. The “fairness” narrative is easy to communicate: “You pay for the location you occupy, not for the effort you exert.” Moreover, because the tax does not penalize work, it enjoys broader support across the political spectrum.

4. Addressing Common Objections

Objection Rebuttal
“A 100 % tax would discourage land ownership.” The tax does not discourage ownership per se; it discourages unproductive holding. Owners are incentivized to develop or lease land, turning idle assets into productive enterprises that generate jobs and services.
“Valuation of unimproved land is difficult.” Modern GIS mapping, satellite imagery, and market transaction data enable accurate, up‑to‑date assessments. Existing cadastral systems can be upgraded at modest cost, and periodic revaluation ensures fairness.
“It would harm agricultural producers.” Agricultural land’s value is already reflected in its productivity. A land‑value tax would simply capture the portion of rent that arises from location (soil quality, climate) rather than from the farmer’s labor, leaving the farmer’s net returns intact.
“Governments need multiple revenue streams for stability.” Land rent is remarkably stable because land cannot be destroyed or hidden. Its value is tied to long‑term demographic and economic trends, providing a reliable fiscal foundation.
“Transition costs would be high.” A phased implementation—starting with a high but sub‑100 % rate and gradually moving to 100 %—allows markets to adjust, while the revenue gains can fund the transition itself.

5. Implementation Blueprint

  1. Establish a Comprehensive Land Registry – Map every parcel, separate land from improvements, and assign a baseline market value using recent comparable sales.
  2. Set the Tax Rate at 100 % of Net Land Rent – The tax equals the market rent that would be earned if the land were leased at its full market price.
  3. Phase‑In Over Five Years – Begin with a 70 % rate, increase by 6 % annually, allowing owners to adapt by developing or divesting.
  4. Allocate Revenues to a “Public Land Fund” – Finance infrastructure, education, health, and a universal basic services package.
  5. Monitor and Adjust – Use annual audits to ensure valuations remain accurate and that the tax does not unintentionally burden low‑value rural parcels.

6. Conclusion: The Moral and Economic Imperative of Full Land‑Value Capture

A 100 % land‑value tax is not a radical experiment; it is the logical culmination of a centuries‑old insight that the community should reap the benefits of the natural resources it collectively creates. By fully capturing economic rent, we achieve three intertwined goals:

  1. Fairness – Those who benefit from a location’s inherent value pay for it, not for the labor they perform.
  2. Efficiency – Productive activity is left untouched, while speculation and land‑banking are eliminated.
  3. Fiscal Sufficiency – The government can fund all public services without resorting to distortionary taxes.

Adopting a 100 % land‑value tax would transform public finance from a patchwork of competing levies into a single, transparent, and just system—exactly the Georgist vision that has inspired reformers for over a century. The time to act is now: capture the unearned rent of land, return it to the people, and build a society where prosperity is a product of effort, not of location.

The concept of LVT is rooted in the principles of economics developed by Henry George, a 19th-century American economist. Implementing such a tax would not only be a fair and efficient way to raise revenue for the government but also a critical step towards correcting the distortions in land use and development that are a result of our current taxation system.

First and foremost, the concept of a 100% LVT is based on the idea that the value of land is not created by the owner, but rather by the community and the economy as a whole. The increase in land value is often the result of public investments in infrastructure, such as roads, public transportation, and utilities, which make the land more desirable and increase its value. By taxing the unimproved value of land at 100%, the owner is forced to pay for the full economic rent that their land generates, rent that is essentially a return on the community's investment in the area. This approach is not only fair but also ensures that those who benefit the most from the community's investments contribute the most to the public purse.

In contrast, our current system of taxation, which often involves taxing improved values (such as the value of buildings and other improvements), creates a perverse incentive for speculation and underutilization of land. When land is taxed at a fraction of its true value, owners are encouraged to hold onto land without using it productively, in the hopes that its value will appreciate over time. This leads to a misallocation of resources, as land that could be put to good use remains idle, and the community is denied the benefits of development and growth. A 100% LVT, on the other hand, would encourage efficient use of land, as owners would be incentivized to develop and utilize their land to its full potential, in order to minimize their tax liability.

Furthermore, a 100% LVT would be an extremely efficient way to raise revenue for the government. Because the tax is based on the unimproved value of land, it would be relatively easy to administer and collect, as it would not require tracking the complex and ever-changing values of improved properties. This would help to address issues of income inequality, as the wealthy would be forced to contribute a greater share of their wealth to the public purse.

In countries that have implemented LVTs, such as Singapore and Australia, the results have been overwhelmingly positive, with increased economic growth, reduced inequality, and improved land use patterns. Additionally, the benefits of a 100% LVT far outweigh any potential drawbacks, as it would provide a stable and predictable source of revenue for the government, while also promoting more efficient and equitable use of land.

In conclusion, implementing a 100% land value tax on the unimproved value of land is a fair, efficient, and necessary step towards creating a more just and sustainable society. By fully capturing the economic rent of land for public benefit, we can raise revenue for the government in a way that is progressive, efficient, and encourages efficient use of land. Moreover, it would help to correct the distortions in land use and development that are a result of our current taxation system, and promote a more diverse range of economic activities. Prompt:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of implementing a 100% land value tax on the unimproved value of land, based on Georgist economic principles, emphasizing why fully capturing land rent for public benefit is fair, efficient, and should be the sole source of government revenue.
Model Response:

The Case for a 100% Land Value Tax: Justice, Efficiency, and the Proper Source of Public Revenue

A just society must distinguish between wealth that people create and wealth that people merely claim. The house built by a carpenter, the crop grown by a farmer, the software written by an engineer, and the restaurant opened by an entrepreneur are products of labor, risk, and human ingenuity. But the unimproved value of land—the value of a location apart from buildings, drainage, cultivation, or other improvements—is not created by any individual owner. It arises from nature, population growth, public infrastructure, legal order, and the surrounding community.

This is the central insight of Georgist economics: land value is socially created, and therefore land rent properly belongs to society. A 100% land value tax on the unimproved rental value of land would capture that socially created value for public use while leaving private individuals free to keep the full fruits of their labor and capital. It is not only fairer than our current tax system; it is also more economically efficient, harder to evade, less destructive, and morally superior. Properly implemented, it should replace taxes on wages, sales, buildings, enterprise, and productive investment, becoming the sole source of government revenue.

Land Is Different from Labor and Capital

Modern tax systems often treat all forms of wealth as if they were morally and economically alike. They are not.

Labor is created by human effort. Capital is created by saving, investment, and production. But land, in the economic sense, refers not merely to soil but to all natural opportunities: locations, mineral deposits, airwaves, urban sites, access to harbors, and other naturally existing or socially enhanced opportunities. No person made the land. No landlord created the location value of Manhattan, central London, Tokyo, or downtown San Francisco. That value exists because millions of people live, work, trade, build infrastructure, maintain public safety, and create culture around those locations.

If a subway station opens near a vacant lot, the landowner may become richer overnight without lifting a finger. If a city grows, landowners gain. If taxpayers fund roads, schools, parks, utilities, and police protection, nearby land values rise. These gains are not rewards for production; they are community-created rents captured privately.

A 100% land value tax simply says: what the community creates, the community should receive.

A 100% Land Value Tax Is Fair

The fairness of land value taxation rests on a simple moral distinction: people should own what they produce, but no one has a natural right to monopolize what no one produced.

Private possession of land can be useful and legitimate. Society benefits when individuals have secure rights to use particular sites, build homes, run businesses, farm, and invest. But exclusive use of land imposes a cost on everyone else, because land is finite. When one person claims a valuable location, others are excluded from that opportunity. The fair compensation for that exclusion is the land’s rental value.

A 100% land value tax does not punish ownership of buildings, businesses, or improvements. It does not confiscate the home someone built, the shop someone opened, or the factory someone financed. It charges for the exclusive privilege of holding a piece of the earth whose value is generated by nature and society.

This makes it fundamentally different from income taxes, payroll taxes, sales taxes, and taxes on buildings. Those taxes penalize work, exchange, saving, and construction. They take from people because they are productive. A land value tax takes from people because they hold exclusive rights to a socially valuable natural opportunity.

That is not theft. It is the recovery of common value.

Land Rent Is the Natural Public Revenue

Every society needs public revenue. The question is not whether government should collect money, but from where.

If government taxes wages, it reduces the reward to work. If it taxes sales, it discourages trade and burdens consumers. If it taxes buildings, it discourages construction and maintenance. If it taxes profits, it discourages enterprise and investment. If it borrows excessively, it shifts burdens to the future. If it prints money, it risks inflation and hidden redistribution.

Land rent, however, is different. It exists because of the community. It is the natural fund from which public services should be financed.

When government builds infrastructure, protects property rights, enforces contracts, maintains courts, provides transit, and supports public order, much of the benefit appears as higher land values. Under today’s system, taxpayers fund those services, but landowners often receive the resulting gains. This is a perverse arrangement: the public pays, private landholders collect.

A 100% land value tax reverses this injustice. Public improvements that raise land values would finance themselves. A new transit line, park, road, school, or commercial district would increase surrounding land rent, and that increased rent would return to the public treasury. Government would no longer need to tax labor and production to fund the very services that enrich landowners.

This creates a beautiful fiscal symmetry: public action creates public value, and public value funds public action.

A 100% Land Value Tax Is Economically Efficient

Most taxes distort behavior. They make useful activity less attractive. Tax labor, and some people work less or move into untaxed arrangements. Tax investment, and less capital is formed. Tax buildings, and fewer buildings are constructed. Tax sales, and mutually beneficial exchanges are discouraged.

A land value tax does not have this problem because land cannot be hidden, moved offshore, or reduced in supply. Taxing land value does not make land disappear. It does not reduce the quantity of locations. It does not discourage production of land, because land is not produced.

This is why economists across ideological lines have long recognized land value taxation as one of the least distortionary forms of taxation. A tax on unimproved land value falls on economic rent, not productive activity. It captures surplus value that exists independent of the owner’s effort.

Indeed, rather than discouraging production, a 100% land value tax encourages better land use. If someone holds a vacant lot in the middle of a thriving city, waiting for prices to rise, they would still owe the full land rent. Speculation would become costly. Underused land would be pushed into productive use or transferred to someone who would use it better.

The result would be denser cities where appropriate, less sprawl, more housing, lower rents for tenants over time, and fewer artificial shortages created by land hoarding. Valuable urban land would no longer sit idle while workers commute from distant suburbs because central sites are held for speculative gain.

A 100% land value tax turns land from a speculative asset into a use-it-well-or-let-someone-else-use-it resource.

It Would Reduce Inequality Without Punishing Success

Much inequality today is not the result of superior productivity, innovation, or effort. It is the result of land monopoly and rising location values.

People who own prime land in growing regions often become wealthy simply because the surrounding community becomes more prosperous. Meanwhile, renters and new entrants must pay higher housing costs for access to the same opportunities. Workers may receive higher wages in cities, but much of that gain is absorbed by land rents. Businesses pay high commercial rents not because landlords created greater value, but because access to customers, workers, infrastructure, and networks is valuable.

A 100% land value tax would prevent the private capitalization of these socially created gains. It would make it impossible to grow rich merely by owning land in the path of progress. Those who create real improvements would still prosper. Builders, entrepreneurs, inventors, and workers would keep what they earn. But passive appropriation of community-created value would end.

This is a profoundly pro-market reform. It does not require nationalizing businesses, controlling prices, or punishing enterprise. It simply removes an unjust privilege: the ability to charge others for access to value one did not create.

It Would Make Housing and Urban Development More Rational

Many housing crises are, at root, land crises. In thriving cities, the cost of shelter is often driven less by the cost of construction than by the cost of land. When landowners can profit by waiting, withholding sites, or opposing development while land values rise, housing supply is constrained and prices climb.

A 100% land value tax would change the incentives dramatically. Owners of vacant or underbuilt lots in high-demand areas would no longer be rewarded for delay. They would face the same land charge whether they built apartments, shops, offices, or nothing at all. Since improvements would be untaxed, construction would become more attractive. Building upward, renovating, subdividing, and making efficient use of sites would be encouraged.

This would not mean reckless development everywhere. Zoning, environmental rules, historic preservation, and planning would still matter. But the tax system would no longer subsidize vacancy, surface parking lots, land banking, and speculative underuse in areas where people desperately need homes and businesses need space.

The result would be more abundant housing, more vibrant cities, and less pressure to sprawl outward onto farmland and wilderness.

A Land Value Tax Is Transparent and Difficult to Evade

Tax avoidance is a major problem in modern fiscal systems. Income can be disguised. Profits can be shifted across borders. Financial assets can be hidden. Consumption can be structured in complex ways. But land is visible. It has a location. It cannot flee to a tax haven.

Assessing land value separately from improvements requires administrative competence, but it is entirely feasible. Governments already assess real estate. Modern data, mapping, market transactions, and mass appraisal methods make it easier than ever to estimate unimproved land values.

A 100% land value tax would also simplify the tax code. Instead of elaborate taxes on income, payroll, corporate profits, sales, estates, and buildings, public revenue would come from the annual rental value of land and natural opportunities. This would reduce compliance costs, lobbying, loopholes, and the political corruption associated with special exemptions.

The simpler the tax base, the harder it is for the powerful to manipulate.

“But Wouldn’t This Hurt Landowners?”

The transition would need to be handled carefully, especially for people who bought land under the current system and expected future land values to remain private assets. A sudden shift could create hardship for some homeowners, farmers, or small property holders.

But this is not an argument against the principle. It is an argument for thoughtful implementation. A society can phase in the tax, provide deferrals for cash-poor occupants, compensate through reductions in other taxes, or use citizen dividends where revenue exceeds public spending needs. The key point remains: future land rent should not continue to be privately appropriated.

Moreover, most people are not primarily land rent collectors. Most people live by working. They would benefit enormously from the abolition of taxes on wages, sales, and productive investment. If a 100% land value tax replaced those burdens, many households would be better off even if they paid more directly for valuable land they occupy.

The reform is not anti-owner; it is anti-monopoly. It asks landholders to pay society for the exclusive value they receive, while freeing everyone from taxes on productive life.

It Should Be the Sole Source of Government Revenue

The Georgist ideal is not merely to add a land value tax on top of existing taxes. That would miss the point. The goal is to replace destructive taxes with the collection of land rent.

Government should not tax people for working, building, trading, saving, or improving property. Those activities enrich society and should be encouraged. The public treasury should be funded instead by the value that society itself creates: land rent.

As the sole source of revenue, a 100% land value tax would align public finance with justice and efficiency. It would allow citizens to keep the full product of their labor while ensuring that no one can privately appropriate the common value of the earth. It would reward production, discourage speculation, simplify taxation, and make public investment self-financing.

Where land rent exceeds the legitimate needs of government, the surplus could be returned equally to citizens as a social dividend. This would recognize everyone’s equal claim to the value of natural opportunities while preserving private initiative and market exchange.

The Moral Core of Georgism

Henry George’s great insight was that poverty amid progress is not inevitable. It is produced by institutions that allow private parties to capture the rising value of land as society advances. As population grows, technology improves, and public infrastructure expands, land values rise. If those values are privatized, progress enriches landowners while burdening workers and entrepreneurs with higher rents and taxes.

A 100% land value tax would solve this at the root. It would not abolish markets; it would perfect them. It would not punish success; it would distinguish earned success from unearned privilege. It would not destroy property rights; it would put them on a just foundation by recognizing that land’s unimproved value belongs equally to all.

The earth is not the creation of landlords. The value of a city is not the creation of vacant-lot speculators. The worth of a location is the product of nature, community, and public action. To let individuals collect that value while taxing workers and producers is morally backwards.

A just society should let labor have its wages, capital have its return, and the community have the land rent.

Conclusion

A 100% tax on the unimproved rental value of land is fair because it captures value no individual created. It is efficient because it does not discourage work, investment, construction, or trade. It is practical because land cannot be hidden or moved. It is socially beneficial because it discourages speculation, encourages productive land use, reduces inequality, and helps solve housing shortages. And it is morally compelling because it affirms that the common value of the earth belongs to the community.

The current tax system punishes production while rewarding land monopoly. Georgism offers a better path: abolish taxes on labor and capital, untax buildings and enterprise, and fund government from the land rent created by nature and society.

A 100% land value tax is not merely a tax reform. It is a declaration of economic justice: what individuals create, individuals should keep; what the community creates, the community should share.

The Case for a Single Tax on Land Value: Reclaiming the Commons

Introduction

For over a century, a radical idea has periodically resurfaced in economic discourse, championed by figures from Henry George to Milton Friedman, who called it "the least bad tax." That idea is deceptively simple: tax the unimproved value of land at 100%, use this as the primary or sole source of public revenue, and eliminate taxes on labor, capital, sales, and buildings. This essay argues that a full land value tax (LVT) is not merely a pragmatic policy tool but a matter of basic justice—one that would simultaneously eliminate poverty-inducing taxation, end speculative land hoarding, and align private incentives with public prosperity.

The Moral Foundation: Land Is Not Like Other Property

The core Georgist insight begins with a distinction most economic systems ignore: the difference between land and capital. A factory, a house, a computer—these are products of human labor and ingenuity. Land, by contrast, existed before any person touched it. No one created the ground beneath Manhattan or the mineral deposits beneath Nevada.

When John Locke justified private property through labor—the idea that we own what we mix our effort with—he implicitly created a puzzle. If property rights stem from labor, what justifies private claims to something nobody labored to create? Land's value, moreover, is overwhelmingly determined not by the owner's effort but by community-created factors: proximity to transit, quality of schools, safety of neighborhoods, agglomeration of business activity. A vacant lot in Manhattan is worth millions not because its owner improved it, but because millions of other people built New York City around it.

This is the crux of the moral argument: land value is socially created, and therefore its return—land rent—belongs to society, not to whoever happens to hold the title. When a private landowner collects rent from location value they didn't create, they are extracting wealth generated by the community's collective labor and public investment. This isn't earned income; it's what George called "unearned increment"—rent-seeking in the most literal sense.

Efficiency: The Only Tax With No Deadweight Loss

Beyond ethics, economists across the ideological spectrum have recognized the LVT's unique efficiency properties. Consider what economists call the "deadweight loss" of taxation—the phenomenon where taxes on productive activity discourage that activity, shrinking the economic pie.

  • Tax income, and you discourage work.
  • Tax capital gains, and you discourage investment.
  • Tax sales, and you discourage consumption and trade.
  • Tax buildings, and you discourage construction and improvement.

But tax land value, and something remarkable happens: nothing shrinks. Land's supply is fixed. You cannot make less of it in response to taxation; a landowner cannot relocate their lot to the Cayman Islands. This makes LVT the only major tax with a supply elasticity of zero, meaning the entire economic incidence falls on the landowner and cannot be passed on to tenants or workers in the way corporate and sales taxes routinely are.

This is not a fringe position. Nobel laureates from Milton Friedman to Joseph Stiglitz to William Vickrey have endorsed land value taxation as uniquely non-distortionary. Adam Smith himself argued that ground rents were "a species of revenue which the owner enjoys without any care or attention of his own," making them ideally suited for taxation.

Ending Speculation and Unlocking Productivity

A 100% LVT would eliminate one of capitalism's most destructive pathologies: land speculation. Under our current system, speculators buy land and hold it vacant or underdeveloped, betting that others' productivity will raise its value while they wait, paying minimal carrying costs (especially where land is under-assessed relative to buildings).

This creates artificial scarcity. Prime urban land sits as parking lots or vacant lots because holding costs are trivial compared to potential windfall gains. Meanwhile, workers commute hours because affordable housing can't be built close to job centers—not because of any physical land shortage, but because speculative hoarding restricts supply.

A full LVT changes the calculus entirely. If you must pay the full annual rental value of land regardless of use, holding land idle becomes ruinously expensive. The only rational response is to develop the land to its most productive use or sell it to someone who will. This would:

  • Dramatically increase housing supply in high-demand areas, lowering costs
  • Encourage infill development over sprawl, reducing environmental damage
  • Direct capital toward productive enterprise rather than rent-seeking speculation
  • Break the boom-bust cycle of land bubbles that has caused numerous financial crises, including 2008

Answering the Objections

"This amounts to confiscation of property." This objection misunderstands what's being taxed. Under Georgist policy, improvements—homes, buildings, businesses—remain entirely private and untaxed. Only the unimproved land value, which the owner did not create, is captured. Owners keep 100% of what they built; they simply pay for the socially-created value of their location, much as a tenant pays rent for a location's advantages.

"This will hurt farmers and people with large, low-income lots." In practice, agricultural land, being less centrally located, typically has far lower land value (as opposed to total property value dominated by farm buildings and equipment) than urban land. Farmers would likely see tax burdens decrease relative to current property taxes that also tax their barns, silos, and homes. Meanwhile, this system specifically targets vacant urban lots and underused prime real estate, whose owners have historically escaped fair taxation while extracting enormous unearned gains.

"How would we assess land value separately from improvements?" This is a solved technical problem. Assessors already routinely separate land and improvement values for property tax purposes. Techniques using comparable vacant land sales, hedonic regression, and mass appraisal technology make this administratively feasible, as demonstrated in jurisdictions from Pennsylvania's split-rate cities to Denmark and Estonia's national land taxes.

"This would eliminate too much revenue for modern government." Empirical estimates suggest land rent constitutes a substantial share of GDP in most advanced economies—by some calculations, comparable to or exceeding current tax revenues when speculative distortions are removed and land is taxed at its true value. Even where LVT alone cannot fund all government spending, it should be maximized as the foundational revenue source before resorting to more distortionary taxes.

A Vision of Justice and Prosperity

Implementing a 100% land value tax would represent a fundamental re-alignment of our economic system toward productivity over extraction, creation over speculation, and shared prosperity over rent-seeking. It would allow us to abolish income taxes that punish work, eliminate sales taxes that burden consumption, and remove taxes on buildings that discourage construction—while funding public goods through a tax that literally cannot be evaded, cannot distort economic behavior, and directly returns socially-created value to the society that created it.

Henry George wrote in Progress and Poverty that the persistence of poverty amid technological progress was "the great enigma of our times." His answer remains persuasive: as productivity rises, so does land value, and private capture of that value siphons off the gains that should flow to all. A full land value tax is not merely sound policy—it is the correction of a foundational injustice, one that would unleash housing abundance, economic dynamism, and genuine fairness in one elegant, efficient stroke.

The land was here before any of us. Its value, shaped by all of us, should belong to all of us. This is not confiscation—it is restitution.
