The earth is our common inheritance. Not mine. Not yours. Not any corporation's or government's. It belongs equally to every human being ever born and ever to be born. It is the foundation upon which all life depends.

When we allow private individuals to monopolize this inheritance—to demand payment from their fellow humans simply for permission to exist on this planet—we commit an injustice so profound that no amount of custom can sanctify it.

The child born today, in a world where all land is already claimed, has no inheritance. They come into the world naked and propertyless, with no claim on the earth itself. They must pay—to landlords who did not create the land—simply for a place to stand.

This is wrong.

But it is not inevitable! We can choose differently. We can choose a world where the gift of nature is shared equally. Where no one pays tribute to another for what neither created. Where labor is free, enterprise is free, and the common heritage funds the common good.

The Path Forward

I do not expect this transformation tomorrow. Great injustices are not overthrown in a day. The powers that benefit from land monopoly are vast and will resist with all their might.

But truth is more powerful than vested interest. Justice is more compelling than tradition. And the promise of a world without poverty amid plenty—a world where work is rewarded and monopoly is abolished—is more inspiring than any defense of the status quo.

Begin locally. Cities can adopt land value taxation. States can shift from property taxes on buildings to taxes on land alone. Each step proves the wisdom of the policy. Each reform demonstrates its benefits.

Speak to your neighbors. Teach them what Henry George taught us. Show them the injustice hidden in plain sight. Let them see that they are robbed every month, every paycheck, every rent check—robbed of what they create and robbed of what is rightfully theirs.

And vote. Organize. Demand. Make politicians choose: Will they stand with the landless, the workers, the creators? Or will they defend the privilege of those who produce nothing and take everything?

Conclusion: A Vision of the Possible

Close your eyes. Imagine.

America, twenty years hence. The income tax is a memory. The payroll tax is forgotten. The IRS is a skeleton of its former self.

Workers keep what they earn. Entrepreneurs keep what they create. Every incentive rewards production, creation, contribution.

Our cities are alive. Vacant lots have become apartments, shops, parks. Young families buy homes without crippling thirty-year mortgages. Neighborhoods flourish.

The land speculator is extinct. It is no longer profitable to hold valuable land idle, to squeeze communities, to profit from scarcity. Land is available for its best use because the tax ensures it.

And funding our government? A single, simple tax on land values. Unavoidable. Just. Efficient. Collecting what belongs to all of us—the value that we together create—and returning it to our common treasury.

This is not a dream. This is the logical consequence of a simple moral truth: What we produce is ours; what nature provides belongs to all.

Henry George saw this truth. Albert Einstein endorsed it. Martin Luther King Jr. embraced it. Economists from Adam Smith to Milton Friedman acknowledged the justice and efficiency of land value taxation.

Now it is our turn.

Will we continue to punish labor and reward monopoly? Will we continue to tax the builder and exempt the land hoarder? Will we continue to impoverish the many to enrich the idle few?

Or will we, at last, proclaim the truth that sets us free: The land belongs to the people!

The choice is ours. The time is now. The cause is just.

Let us claim our inheritance. Let us tax the land. Let us make poverty a relic of history.

Thank you.

Model Response:

The Earth Belongs to Everyone: The Case for a 100% Land Value Tax

A Comprehensive Defense of Georgist Public Finance

Introduction: The Problem Hidden in Plain Sight

There is a peculiar injustice at the heart of modern economies that we have grown so accustomed to that we rarely think to question it. Every morning, millions of working people rise early, commute to jobs, exercise their talents, build businesses, and create value through the labor of their minds and bodies. Every evening, a separate class of people collects rent checks, watches land values appreciate, and accumulates wealth not through any productive effort of their own but simply by holding legal title to pieces of the earth — pieces of the earth they did not create, did not improve, and contribute nothing toward maintaining. The first group is taxed heavily for its productivity. The second group is rewarded handsomely for its passivity. We call this arrangement a free market economy.

It is nothing of the sort.

The proposal I will defend in these pages is radical in its simplicity and simple in its radicalism: the unimproved value of land — not the buildings on it, not the improvements to it, but the bare locational value of the land itself — should be taxed at 100%, with the revenue distributed either as public services or as a universal dividend to all citizens, and this single tax should replace all other government revenue sources. This is the central proposal of Henry George, articulated with stunning moral clarity in his 1879 masterwork Progress and Poverty, and it remains one of the most compelling, rigorously defensible, and persistently neglected reform proposals in the history of political economy.

The case for the land value tax (LVT) rests on three pillars: justice, efficiency, and sufficiency. Land rent is morally owed to the community because the community creates it. A 100% land value tax is the most economically efficient tax imaginable because it cannot reduce the supply of land or distort productive behavior. And the total rental value of land is sufficient — more than sufficient — to fund the legitimate functions of government. Each of these pillars deserves careful examination, and each, upon examination, proves stronger than its critics suppose.

Part One: The Moral Foundation — Who Created the Value of Land?

Before evaluating the economics of land value taxation, we must grapple with a prior question that economics alone cannot answer: who is morally entitled to the value that land generates? This is not a technical question. It is a question about justice, about property rights at their most fundamental level, and getting it wrong has consequences that radiate through every subsequent policy choice.

The Lockean Problem and Its Resolution

The philosophical tradition most commonly invoked to defend private property is Lockean — John Locke argued in his Second Treatise that individuals acquire legitimate property rights by "mixing their labor" with natural resources. If you cultivate a field, build a house, or forge a tool, you have a claim to the fruits of that effort. This principle is intuitively compelling and forms the bedrock of our intuitions about ownership. But Locke himself recognized an important limitation: this labor-mixing theory justifies ownership only when "there is enough and as good left in common for others." This is the Lockean proviso, and in a world of finite land in finite desirable locations, it is violated every time someone claims exclusive private ownership of a piece of earth.

Henry George resolved this tension more elegantly than Locke himself. George did not oppose private property in the fruits of labor — he was one of its most passionate defenders. What he opposed was the privatization of something that no individual labored to create. Land is not a product of human effort. Its existence precedes humanity. The value of a specific parcel of land, moreover, is not created by the landowner but by the surrounding community — by the infrastructure government builds, by the businesses that locate nearby, by the workers who make the area productive, by the sheer density of human civilization that makes certain locations more valuable than others. When a city invests in a new subway line and property values along the route skyrocket, the landowners along that route have done nothing to earn that increase. The community created it; the community should capture it.

This is not a novel or extreme position. It follows directly from the most basic principles of desert-based property theory. You are entitled to what you create. You are not entitled to what others create. Since the community creates land value through its collective presence and investment, the community is entitled to land value. The landowner who pockets ground rent is, in the most precise philosophical sense, taking something that belongs to others. The land value tax does not confiscate private property; it returns to the community what was never legitimately private in the first place.

Common Ownership and the Citizen's Birthright

There is an even more foundational moral argument for public capture of land rent, one articulated by thinkers from Thomas Paine to contemporary philosophers like Peter Vallentyne and Hillel Steiner. The earth, in its natural state, is the common inheritance of humanity. No one earned the right to be born. No one chose their country or their city. Access to the natural world — including the locational advantages that arise from the presence of civilization — is something every human being is owed simply by virtue of being human.

When we allow some individuals to monopolize pieces of the earth and charge others for access, we are permitting a form of appropriation that harms those who are excluded. Every person who pays rent to a private landlord is paying for the right to occupy a portion of the earth that, in justice, belongs to all. A 100% land value tax, with revenues returned to citizens as a universal dividend or public services, is the mechanism by which this original entitlement is honored. It is the rent we all pay to each other for the exclusive use of land that belongs to us all.

Thomas Paine made this argument with characteristic directness in his 1797 pamphlet Agrarian Justice: "It is the value of the improvement only, and not the earth itself, that is individual property. Every proprietor, therefore, of cultivated land, owes to the community a ground-rent for the land which he holds." Paine proposed funding a universal basic income from this source — a proposal that was radical in 1797 and is fashionable today, yet whose most logical funding mechanism, land value taxation, remains strangely controversial.

Against the Objection of Purchaser Innocence

The most emotionally compelling objection to full land value taxation is the claim that current landowners purchased their land in good faith at market prices and therefore have a legitimate claim to its value. This objection deserves a direct and serious response.

First, we must distinguish between the purchase price of land and the ongoing rental stream it generates. When a landowner buys land, she purchases access to future ground rents. Under a 100% LVT, those future ground rents are returned to the community. The purchase price paid in anticipation of those rents was, under current law, the price of something the purchaser was never justly entitled to. As economist Mason Gaffney has argued extensively, the capitalized value of land reflects the community's failure to collect what it was owed. Paying a price for stolen goods does not establish a clean title.

Second, and more practically, the transition to a full LVT need not be abrupt. A phased implementation — increasing the land value tax rate gradually over a decade or more while simultaneously reducing other taxes — would allow current landowners to adjust. Those who purchased land primarily as productive inputs (farmers, manufacturers, small business owners) would find their overall tax burden reduced as income and sales taxes are eliminated. Those who purchased land purely as a rent-seeking investment would face declining returns, but this is precisely what justice demands: the elimination of unearned income streams at the expense of productive activity.

Part Two: The Efficiency Case — Why the Land Value Tax Is Uniquely Non-Distortionary

If the moral case for land value taxation rested on justice alone, it would still be compelling. But the economic case adds a dimension that transforms the LVT from a merely just policy into what Nobel laureate William Vickrey called "the most perfect tax" in existence. The land value tax does not just avoid economic harm — it actively promotes economic health in ways that no other revenue instrument can match.

The Golden Rule of Taxation: Don't Tax What You Want More Of

Every tax imposes a burden not just in the revenue it collects but in the behavioral changes it induces. Tax labor and you discourage work. Tax capital investment and you discourage investment. Tax consumption and you discourage exchange. Tax corporate profits and you discourage enterprise. Every conventional revenue source punishes some form of productive activity, creating what economists call "deadweight loss" — a reduction in economic welfare that benefits no one. These losses are not trivial; estimates of the deadweight loss from the American tax system run to hundreds of billions of dollars annually.

A tax on the unimproved value of land is structurally different. Land cannot be created by human effort, and therefore cannot be created in response to a tax incentive. The supply of land is perfectly inelastic. This is not a complication or an assumption — it is a physical fact about the nature of land. You cannot manufacture more Manhattan. You cannot produce more frontage on San Francisco Bay. Taxing land value therefore cannot reduce the supply of land, cannot induce landowners to produce less land, and cannot create any of the distortions that afflict every other form of taxation.

This is the fundamental insight of public finance economics as applied to land: because the supply is fixed, the entire incidence of a land value tax falls on landowners, and none of it can be passed on to tenants through higher rents or to consumers through higher prices. A landlord who tries to raise rents in response to an LVT will find no shortage of competing landlords offering lower rents, because the supply of land has not changed. The market rent for land is determined by demand, not by what landlords wish to charge, and a tax that takes the landowner's rent away does not change the demand for land.

The Productivity Bonus: Taxing Idleness, Rewarding Use

The benefits of a full LVT go beyond the absence of distortion. Because the tax must be paid regardless of whether the land is productively used, it creates a powerful incentive to put land to its highest and best use. Under current systems, landowners frequently benefit from holding land vacant or underutilized, waiting for values to rise while contributing nothing to the community. This speculation is economically devastating. In cities across America and around the world, valuable land near transit hubs, employment centers, and amenities sits vacant or dramatically underutilized because speculators are waiting for the right moment to sell. Meanwhile, workers must commute from distant suburbs, housing costs spiral out of control, and productive investment is crowded out by the expectation of passive capital gains.

A 100% land value tax demolishes this speculative logic completely. When ground rent flows to the public rather than the private landowner, holding land idle becomes immediately expensive. Every day a valuable urban lot sits as a parking lot rather than housing or commercial space costs the owner the full rental value of the land. The incentive to develop promptly becomes overwhelming. Land that was hoarded for speculation suddenly floods the market for productive use. Housing supply expands. Commercial rents fall. The economy becomes more dynamic and more accessible to new entrants who previously could not afford land costs.

This effect is not theoretical. Jurisdictions that have experimented with higher land value taxes — including certain Pennsylvania cities under their "graded tax" system, Estonia's post-Soviet land tax, various Australian municipalities, and the special case of Singapore — have consistently observed increased development of previously underutilized land, greater housing availability, and more dynamic local economies. The evidence is fragmentary because full LVT has never been implemented at scale, but every partial experiment points in the same direction.

The Business Climate Revolution

Consider what eliminating all other taxes in favor of a land value tax would mean for the productive economy. Income taxes, payroll taxes, sales taxes, capital gains taxes, corporate taxes, excise taxes, estate taxes — all gone. Replaced by a single annual assessment on the unimproved value of land.

The implications are extraordinary. Every dollar earned through labor would be kept in full. Every dollar invested in capital equipment, software, research, or human development would escape taxation. Every transaction in the economy would be untaxed. The enormous compliance burden of the current tax system — the accountants, tax lawyers, lobbyists, and corporate tax departments whose entire existence is devoted to navigating a Byzantine revenue code — would be largely eliminated. Entrepreneurship, always the most important driver of economic dynamism, would face no tax penalty. The only thing taxed would be the exclusive appropriation of land — which is not a productive contribution to the economy but a claim on the productive contributions of others.

The economist's term for the current tax system is that it is "allocatively distorting." Our tax code actively encourages economically irrational behavior — holding land vacant, incorporating in Delaware, structuring compensation as capital gains rather than wages, locating factories in tax havens rather than optimal locations — all to minimize tax liability rather than maximize productive output. A land value tax eliminates these distortions wholesale. The economy would allocate resources based on productivity, not tax arbitrage.

Addressing the Capitalization Objection

Critics sometimes argue that because a 100% LVT would eliminate all private ground rent, it would reduce land to zero market value, destroying the collateral basis for loans secured against land and triggering a financial crisis. This is a serious objection that deserves a careful response.

The concern about collateral is real but overstated. Under a full LVT, the value of land itself approaches zero (since the stream of rents has been captured publicly), but the value of improvements on land — buildings, infrastructure, capital investment — is entirely unaffected and indeed increases as productive activity is rewarded. Mortgage lending secured against buildings continues uninterrupted. The financial sector's healthy activities are preserved; only the speculative extraction of ground rent is eliminated.

The transition question — what happens to the trillions of dollars of existing land value during the shift to LVT? — is legitimate and requires careful policy design. Phased implementation, as noted above, prevents a sudden collapse of land prices. Alternatively, some Georgist thinkers have proposed issuing landowners bonds in exchange for their land titles, with bond payments funded from LVT revenues and declining over time as the transition completes. The details of transition management are important policy questions, but they are not arguments against the destination. We do not refuse to correct an unjust arrangement merely because correction requires careful management.

Part Three: The Sufficiency Case — Can Land Rent Really Fund Government?

Perhaps the most common empirical objection to the Georgist single tax proposal is that land rent is simply not large enough to replace all other revenue sources. This objection is repeated so frequently and confidently that many people assume it has been definitively established. It has not. The evidence, properly examined, suggests that total land rent in modern economies is very large — large enough to fund government, and perhaps larger than commonly supposed.

The Rent of the United States: What Do We Know?

Estimating total land rent is methodologically challenging because land and improvements are rarely assessed separately in modern property tax systems, and because the full rental value of land includes not just what is actually paid in rent but the implicit rent of owner-occupied properties and the value of publicly held land. Nevertheless, serious researchers have attempted these estimates, and their findings are striking.

The economist Steven Cord estimated in the 1980s that land rent in the United States amounted to approximately 25-30% of national income. More recent estimates by Michael Hudson, Mason Gaffney, and Fred Harrison suggest the figure may be considerably higher when properly accounting for resource rents, spectrum rents, and other natural monopoly rents. The economist Josh Ryan-Collins and colleagues, in their book Rethinking the Economics of Land and Housing, document the extraordinary growth of land values relative to GDP in recent decades. The Federal Reserve's Flow of Funds data suggests total U.S. real estate value of approximately $50 trillion, of which land likely represents 40-60% — or $20-30 trillion in total land value. At a modest capitalization rate of 4%, this implies annual land rent on the order of $800 billion to $1.2 trillion.

Federal government revenues in 2023 were approximately $4.4 trillion, suggesting that land rent alone, at conventional estimates, falls short. But several important considerations expand the calculation significantly.

First, current land value estimates are themselves suppressed by the expectation that owners will capture future rents. Under a 100% LVT, the entire future rent stream belongs to the public, and the tax base should be calculated on the full potential rental value, not the currently observed market rent net of existing taxes. Second, resource rents — the value of oil, gas, minerals, spectrum, ocean fisheries, water rights, and other natural resources — are enormous and should properly be included in any comprehensive land value taxation scheme. Third, as LVT eliminates distortions and stimulates economic productivity, the tax base expands as more economic activity occurs and land is used more intensively. Fourth, reduced government waste, which current tax complexity enables through lobbying and special provisions, would allow the same services to be funded with lower total revenues.

A comprehensive land and resource rent tax would, by credible estimates, cover a very substantial portion of current government expenditure — perhaps most of it. Where modest gaps remain, they could be addressed by reducing government activities that are themselves distortionary or wasteful, by user fees for specific services, or by small adjustments in the LVT rate.

The Sufficiency Point Made Differently

Even if we concede for purposes of argument that land rent falls somewhat short of covering all current government expenditure, the proper response is not to abandon the land value tax but to ask what combination of revenue sources creates the least economic harm. The answer to this question is unambiguous: land value taxation causes zero deadweight loss, while every other tax causes positive deadweight loss. The optimal strategy is therefore to exhaust the land rent base entirely before turning to any other revenue source. This is not a radical conclusion — it follows straightforwardly from the standard economic theory of optimal taxation.

We currently do the opposite. We leave enormous amounts of ground rent uncaptured in private hands while taxing labor, capital, and consumption heavily. This is backwards in precisely the way that makes our economies less productive, less dynamic, and more unequal than they need to be.

Part Four: The Inequality Crisis and the Georgist Solution

We live in an era of extraordinary and growing economic inequality. The share of income captured by the top 1% has risen dramatically in most developed countries over the past four decades. The wealth gap between the asset-owning class and wage earners has widened to levels not seen since the Gilded Age. Housing costs have risen far faster than wages in virtually every major city, making the dream of homeownership increasingly distant for younger generations.

These are not accidents of the market. They are predictable consequences of a policy framework that allows private capture of socially-created land value. As cities become more productive and desirable, the value of urban land rises. This value accrues entirely to those who already own property, while those who do not — renters, recent graduates, immigrants, workers in expensive cities — pay ever-higher fractions of their income for housing. The mechanism of increasing inequality is, to a striking extent, the mechanism of rising land rents captured privately.

Henry George saw this with prophetic clarity in 1879: "The reason why, in spite of the increase of productive power, wages constantly tend to a minimum which will give but a bare living, is that, with increase in productive power, rent tends to even greater increase, thus producing a constant tendency to the forcing down of wages." We have built a society in which economic growth primarily benefits landowners, and we then express bafflement at growing inequality. The Georgist analysis not only diagnoses the disease but prescribes the cure.

A 100% land value tax would compress inequality through every mechanism simultaneously. It would eliminate the primary vehicle of passive wealth accumulation — rising land values. It would reduce housing costs dramatically as land speculation ends and development increases. It would allow the elimination of taxes on wages, raising the take-home pay of every working person. And if LVT revenues were distributed as a universal basic income — as Paine proposed and contemporary advocates like Matt Bruenig and Peter Barnes have elaborated — it would provide a floor of economic security for every citizen, regardless of employment status.

This is not redistribution in the conventional sense, in which taxes collected from productive activity are transferred to others. It is the restoration of what should have always belonged to everyone — the value created by our common civilization — to all the members of that civilization.

Part Five: Responding to the Major Objections

No serious policy proposal escapes serious objection, and the 100% land value tax faces several that deserve careful engagement rather than dismissal.

"It Would Destroy Small Farmers and Longtime Homeowners"

The image of the elderly widow on a fixed income, unable to pay a substantial land value tax on the family home she has lived in for fifty years, is perhaps the most emotionally powerful objection to LVT. It is worth taking seriously — and then noting that it is entirely solvable.

Several mechanisms are available. Tax deferral allows landowners to defer payment of LVT until the property is sold, at which point the accumulated liability is settled from the proceeds. This eliminates the cash flow problem entirely — the widow keeps her home until she chooses to sell, and the community recovers its rent at that point. For agricultural land, LVT provides powerful incentives to farm efficiently and discourages the conversion of farmland to speculative holdings, which is actually better for small farmers than the current system. Homestead exemptions for primary residences up to a certain value could be incorporated into the transition framework without significantly undermining the overall logic.

The concern about farmers and longtime homeowners is a transition concern, not an objection to the principle. It should be addressed with thoughtful transition policy, not used to preserve a fundamentally unjust arrangement indefinitely.

"Land Valuation Is Too Difficult to Administer"

Critics argue that separating the value of land from the value of improvements is technically complex and prone to manipulation. This objection is empirically weak. Land valuation is performed routinely in jurisdictions that maintain split-rate property taxes, and methods for assessing unimproved land value — using comparable sales of vacant land, subtracting depreciated replacement cost of buildings from total property value, using mass appraisal techniques — are well-developed in both practice and theory.

Indeed, a full LVT simplifies administration compared to the current system in important respects. There is no need to assess improvements separately from land once improvements are untaxed. Computational methods for mass land appraisal have improved enormously with geographic information systems and big data analytics. Singapore manages one of the world's most sophisticated land valuation systems efficiently. The technical challenge is real but manageable — certainly far less complex than the current corporate tax code.

"It Would Cause Political Backlash from Landowners"

This is perhaps the most honest objection: landowners are a powerful political constituency, and policies that significantly reduce their wealth will face fierce opposition. This is undeniably true. It is also entirely beside the point as an objection to the justice and efficiency of the policy. Many just and efficient reforms face political opposition from those who benefit from current injustice. The appropriate response is to make the moral and economic case more clearly and build a political coalition around the genuine interests of the majority — workers, renters, entrepreneurs — who stand to benefit enormously.

It is worth noting that homeowners — who are often conflated with landowners in this debate — would not necessarily be net losers under LVT. If a homeowner's LVT liability is less than the income tax and payroll tax they currently pay, and if the LVT is accompanied by a universal dividend or substantially improved public services, many homeowners would be better off. The losers are concentrated in the class of large landowners who hold significant ground rent claims — a small and extraordinarily wealthy group.

Conclusion: The Simple Truth Behind the Complexity

Henry George was not a complicated thinker. His central insight can be stated in a paragraph. The value of land is created by the community — by the presence of people, institutions, infrastructure, and civilization. That which the community creates should benefit the community. We should tax the community's creation — land value — and not tax what individuals create — the fruits of their labor and enterprise. Everything else in Georgist thought is elaboration of this simple truth.

The 100% land value tax is not an extremist proposal. It is the logical extension of principles that most people already accept in fragmentary form — that property taxes are more economically neutral than income taxes, that land speculation distorts cities, that passive income should not be more lightly taxed than labor income, that the earth belongs to everyone. Georgism takes these intuitions seriously and follows them to their conclusions.

We stand at a moment when the failures of existing arrangements are impossible to ignore. Housing is unaffordable for the young and the poor. Inequality is extreme and worsening. Urban cores are hollowed by speculation while workers are pushed to unsustainable distances. Tax complexity privileges those who can afford sophisticated avoidance strategies over those who cannot. These are not isolated problems — they are symptoms of a single underlying pathology: the private appropriation of value that rightfully belongs to the community.

The 100% land value tax is the cure. It is just, because it returns to the community what the community created. It is efficient, because it is the only tax that does not distort productive behavior. It is sufficient, because the earth's bounty, properly accounted, is ample to fund the common welfare. And it is achievable, because the political majority — the renters, workers, and entrepreneurs who bear the heaviest burden of the current system — have every reason to demand it.

Henry George believed that poverty in the midst of progress was not natural, not inevitable, not even particularly mysterious. It was the predictable consequence of a specific institutional choice — the private appropriation of ground rent — and it could be ended by reversing that choice. A century and a half later, with inequality at historic highs and housing at historic lows of affordability, his diagnosis reads not as period radicalism but as precise and urgent analysis.

The earth belongs to us all. It is time our tax system reflected that truth.

Georgist Land Value Tax: Core Arguments

Background

Henry George articulated this position primarily in Progress and Poverty (1879). The proposal involves taxing the unimproved rental value of land at 100% while eliminating other taxes entirely.

The Central Distinction

Georgists distinguish sharply between:

  • Land - natural resources, location value, electromagnetic spectrum, anything not produced by human effort
  • Capital/Improvements - buildings, infrastructure, productive investments created by human labor
  • Labor - human productive effort

This distinction drives most subsequent arguments.

Claimed Economic Benefits

Eliminating Deadweight Loss

Standard taxation reduces activity it falls on. Taxing wages discourages work. Taxing capital discourages investment. Land, however, has fixed supply - a tax on it cannot reduce the quantity of land. In principle this makes it one of the most economically neutral taxes available, a point accepted by many mainstream economists including Milton Friedman who called it the "least bad tax."

Eliminating Speculative Holding

A significant Georgist argument concerns vacant or underutilized land, particularly in cities. Currently, owners can hold land without developing it while its value increases as surrounding communities grow. A full land value tax makes this costly, creating pressure to either develop land productively or sell to someone who will. Georgists argue this would substantially increase housing supply and reduce urban land prices available for development.

Capturing Community-Created Value

George argued that land value is not created by the landowner but by the surrounding community - population density, public infrastructure, economic activity, geographic advantages. A railway station increases nearby land values without effort from landowners. Taxing this "unearned increment" captures value the community created and returns it to the community.

Reducing Rent-Seeking

Because landowners can profit simply from holding appreciating land, there are incentives to engage in political activity protecting land interests rather than productive economic activity. Georgists argue this distorts investment and political behavior away from genuinely productive ends.

Claimed Social Benefits

Housing Affordability

By pressing underutilized land into productive use and discouraging speculative holding, proponents argue land value taxation would substantially increase housing supply, reducing costs for renters and buyers who currently transfer wealth to landowners.

Reducing Inequality

George argued land ownership concentration was a primary driver of persistent poverty alongside general prosperity - hence the title Progress and Poverty. Since land value is community-created, taxing it fully would socialize that return rather than allowing it to accumulate privately to landowners. Wages and capital returns, being genuinely produced, would remain private.

Simplicity and Transparency

A single tax base is administratively simpler than multiple overlapping taxes. Land cannot be hidden in offshore accounts or complex financial structures, making avoidance more difficult than with income or corporate taxes.

Claimed Political/Philosophical Justifications

Natural Rights Consistency

George and followers argue that individuals own what they produce through labor but cannot have the same claim to what they did not produce. Land existed before human activity. Therefore private collection of land rent represents an extraction from the community that is philosophically distinct from returns on genuine productive effort.

Labor and Capital Liberation

By eliminating taxes on wages and productive investment, Georgists argue the full returns to labor and enterprise would accrue to those who generated them, which they consider more just and more economically stimulating than the current system.

What Mainstream Economics Generally Accepts vs. Questions

Broadly accepted:

  • Land value tax is more economically efficient than most alternatives
  • It would reduce speculative land holding
  • It has relatively low deadweight loss
  • It would increase pressure for land development

More contested:

  • Whether it would raise sufficient revenue to replace all other taxes
  • Whether perfectly distinguishing land value from improvement value is practically achievable
  • Whether 100% taxation would affect land markets in unanticipated ways
  • Whether the philosophical distinction between land and capital is as clean as claimed

Practical Limitations Georgists Acknowledge

Accurate land value assessment separate from improvements is technically challenging. Political opposition from landowners is substantial. Transition effects could be disruptive for people who purchased land at prices incorporating the expectation of keeping appreciation gains.

The philosophy represents a coherent internally consistent framework, and its core efficiency claim is taken seriously in academic economics even by those who reject the single-tax conclusion.

When did we decide that one person could own the Earth itself? Not the buildings they built. Not the crops they planted. Not the businesses they created through genuine effort and ingenuity. But the ground — the raw, unimproved land that existed before any of us drew our first breath, that no human hand created, that nature and society together made valuable?

We have accepted an arrangement so peculiar, so fundamentally unjust, that if we encountered it fresh — with new eyes — we would recognize it immediately as organized theft.

Here is how the system works today: A person buys land in a growing city. They do nothing with it. They don't build. They don't produce. They simply wait. And as the community around them builds schools, lays roads, establishes hospitals, creates culture, attracts businesses — as other people's labor and investment makes that location desirable — our landowner grows wealthy. Enormously, passively, effortlessly wealthy.

Then they charge rent.

And workers — who built everything that made that land valuable — must pay tribute to access the Earth they were born on.

Henry George called this "the great enigma of our times" — why does poverty deepen as civilization advances? Why, in the most productive societies in human history, do we have homelessness alongside empty lots? Why do workers toil harder each decade while a landowning class captures the gains without lifting a finger?

The answer is staring at us from every city block, every inflated rent check, every vacant speculative parcel sitting idle while families are priced out.

We have privatized the commons and called it property rights.

What Land Actually Is

To understand why Land Value Taxation is not merely practical but morally necessary, we must be precise about what land actually is.

Land is not a product of human labor. No one manufactured the soil of Iowa, the harbor of New York, the mineral deposits of Wyoming, the electromagnetic spectrum, or the view of a mountain. These things simply exist. Their value is created entirely by:

  • The community that surrounds them
  • The public infrastructure that serves them
  • The natural features that preceded us all
  • The mere fact of human civilization requiring space

When a tech company moves to a neighborhood and property values soar, the landowners capture that gain. When a city builds a subway station and surrounding land values increase by millions — a well-documented phenomenon — landowners capture that gain. When society collectively generates prosperity, landowners collect the rent.

This is not reward for contribution. This is a legal entitlement to extract value from other people's effort.

The great economists — Adam Smith, David Ricardo, John Stuart Mill, and yes, Henry George — all recognized this fundamental distinction. Land is categorically different from capital. You can create more capital. You cannot create more land.

And that distinction changes everything.

The Proposal: Simple, Radical, Just

Here is what we are proposing, in plain terms:

Tax the unimproved value of land — fully, completely, at 100% of annual rental value — and use those revenues to fund government entirely, eliminating taxes on labor, production, and capital.

Not the buildings. Not the improvements. Not what people do with land. The land itself. Its location value. The value the community created.

If you build a beautiful home, you keep it. If you start a business, your profits are yours. If you work hard and earn a wage, you keep your paycheck.

But if you hold land — if you occupy a location that the community made valuable — you pay the community for that privilege, in proportion to what that location is actually worth.

And here is the beautiful, almost miraculous consequence of this simple change:

Speculation becomes impossible.

Why would you hold vacant land idle, waiting for values to rise, if you owe the full rental value every single year regardless? You wouldn't. You'd either put the land to productive use or you'd sell it to someone who would. The speculative premium evaporates. Land prices fall dramatically. Housing becomes affordable not through subsidies or price controls, but because the incentive to hoard land is eliminated at the root.

The Economic Case Is Overwhelming

I want to address the skeptics directly, because this proposal is sometimes dismissed as utopian. It is not. It is arguably the most rigorously supported proposal in the history of economic thought.

Consider what economists across the ideological spectrum agree on:

Land Value Tax is the least distortionary tax possible. You cannot avoid it by working less, investing less, or producing less. Land cannot be hidden in offshore accounts. Land cannot be shipped to a tax haven. Land sits exactly where it is, and its value is publicly observable.

When you tax income, you discourage work. When you tax capital gains, you discourage investment. When you tax sales, you discourage commerce. But when you tax land value — the unearned, community-created value of location — you discourage nothing productive. You merely reclaim for the community what the community created.

Nobel laureates have endorsed this principle. Milton Friedman — no radical — called the land value tax "the least bad tax." William Vickrey, Joseph Stiglitz, Paul Samuelson — economists who agree on almost nothing else find common ground here.

Why? Because the math is unambiguous. Land is inelastic. You tax it, and the supply of land does not decrease. What does decrease is the incentive to hold it unproductively.

Cities that have implemented even partial land value taxation — Harrisburg, Pennsylvania; parts of Australia; Estonia — have seen dramatic increases in construction, economic activity, and reduced speculative vacancy.

Imagine those effects multiplied by a full implementation.

But let me speak now not to economists but to the people.

Who owns land in America?

The wealthy. The institutionally powerful. Real estate investment trusts. Corporations. Inherited wealth. Whoever got there first, or had capital to buy in early.

Who pays rent?

The young. The working class. Immigrants. Anyone who arrived after the gates of affordable ownership swung shut. The single mother paying 50% of her income for an apartment in a city she helps sustain every day with her labor.

The current system is a machine for transferring wealth from workers to owners of locations. From those who produce to those who merely possess. From the mobile and young to the established and landed.

Every time a neighborhood improves — through community effort, cultural vitality, public investment — rents rise and the community that created that improvement is priced out of it.

This is not a market outcome. It is an injustice laundered through legal convention.

A full land value tax reverses this flow. The value that communities create returns to communities. It funds the schools, infrastructure, and services that make locations valuable in the first place — a virtuous cycle instead of a vicious one.

And here is something profound: because land value is highest in desirable urban locations occupied disproportionately by the wealthy, the land value tax is inherently progressive without any complicated graduated rate structure. The person who owns the downtown skyscraper lot pays enormously. The farmer on rural land pays modestly. The landless worker pays nothing.

"But what about the homeowner who bought their home and built equity?"

I hear this concern, and I take it seriously. A family who purchased a home in good faith, under the existing rules, built their retirement around that appreciation. This is real.

Here is my answer: transition matters, and we can manage it justly.

We are not confiscating anyone's home. We are shifting the basis of taxation from labor and commerce to location value. For homeowners, this means the buildings they own and improvements they've made are untaxed, while the land beneath them — which they didn't create — contributes to public revenue.

For most modest homeowners, particularly outside the most hyper-inflated markets, this transition is manageable, especially as other taxes on their income and consumption disappear simultaneously. Robust deferral mechanisms for elderly homeowners on fixed incomes are entirely feasible and should be part of any serious implementation plan.

The pain of transition is real for some. But consider the alternative: we continue a system that locks future generations out of ownership entirely, that concentrates land wealth in fewer hands each decade, that extracts rent from workers indefinitely. We cannot protect yesterday's windfall at the cost of tomorrow's justice.

"The government can't be trusted with this revenue."

This is a fair concern about governance, not about the principle. "This is communist. This is taking private property."

No. This is precisely the opposite of communism.

Communism abolishes private ownership of productive capital — the factories, tools, and businesses people create. Land Value Taxation leaves all of that entirely in private hands. It is ferociously pro-market for genuinely created wealth.

What it abolishes is something different: the private appropriation of publicly created value. The unearned increment. The location rent generated not by the owner but by society.

John Locke himself, the philosophical father of property rights, specified that appropriation of nature requires leaving "enough, and as good" for others. We have manifestly failed that test. Locke's proviso demands exactly the kind of correction George proposed.

In this world:

A young couple looking for their first home finds that land prices have fallen dramatically — because the speculative premium is gone, because holding vacant land idle is expensive, because the market clears at productive use values rather than speculators' fantasy prices. They buy, they build, they stay.

A small business owner looking for commercial space finds affordable options — because land banking is uneconomical, because vacant storefronts cost their owners real money every year. Neighborhood commerce flourishes.

A worker takes home her full paycheck. No income tax withheld. No payroll tax. Her employer, freed from employment taxes, can afford to hire more people. The incentive to work, to produce, to innovate — undiminished, indeed strengthened.

Cities densify naturally — because dense productive use is the rational response to high land costs, not sprawl and speculation. Transit becomes economically viable. Walkable neighborhoods emerge from market incentives rather than regulatory mandates.

The person who holds downtown Manhattan — whether an individual or a corporation — pays the community handsomely for that extraordinary privilege, and uses it productively or relinquishes it to someone who will.

Rural communities see different effects: modest land values mean modest tax obligations, while the elimination of income and sales taxes makes rural life more economically viable, potentially reversing the hollowing out of small towns.

And most profoundly:

The basic injustice at the heart of our civilization — the injustice that Henry George watched being born in real time as California's land was carved up before new arrivals' eyes — begins to heal.

We stop asking people to pay for the privilege of being alive on this planet. We start collecting only what is genuinely owed: the value of location, which we together created, returned to us together.

I want to close not with economics but with ethics, because ultimately this is a moral argument.

Thomas Paine wrote in Agrarian Justice that the earth in its natural state belongs to mankind collectively, and that whoever encloses it owes the rest of humanity compensation. Not as charity. As right.

We have built a civilization of extraordinary productivity, knowledge, and potential. We have the technology to house everyone. We have the productive capacity to eliminate material deprivation. We have the organizational sophistication to coordinate complex systems.

And yet we have people sleeping on sidewalks while lots sit empty.

We have workers producing wealth that flows upward to landowners.

We have young people locked out of the cities their energy animates.

We have communities investing in their own neighborhoods only to be priced out of them.

This is not scarcity. This is a choice. It is a policy. It can be changed.

Henry George wrote that he had seen the cause of poverty, and it was not in human nature, not in insufficient production, not in inevitable fate. It was in a specific arrangement — the private ownership of the earth's surface value — that could be altered without confiscation, without revolution, with a single elegant reform that every major economist who has examined it has recognized as sound.

We stand today with that reform still unimplemented, still waiting, still representing perhaps the greatest untried idea in political economy.

The land belongs to all of us. Its value — created by our collective presence, our public investments, our shared civilization — should return to all of us.

Tax the land. Free the people.

The Earth is our common inheritance. It is past time we reclaimed it.

Thank you.

Introduction
The global economic landscape is marred by inequality, inefficient resource allocation, and regressive taxation systems that stifle growth and innovation. I. Fairness: Land Rent as a Common Heritage

Land is a finite, non-reproducible resource whose value stems largely from its location and the surrounding community’s efforts. The prosperity of a city, the infrastructure of a town, and even the demand for rural acreage are collective achievements, not individual ones. A landowner reaps unearned windfalls from rising land values caused by public investments—schools, transit, parks—without contributing to the underlying value. Taxing this unimproved land value rectifies this injustice by redirecting community-generated wealth to the public coffers.

Georgist economics distinguishes between land (nature’s bounty) and improvements (human-made structures). Taxing improvements penalizes productivity and innovation; taxing land, however, acknowledges that private ownership of a common resource necessitates compensation to society. This aligns with the ethical principle that land, a gift of nature, ought to be held in trust for all, not monopolized for private gain. By capturing 100% of land rent, we dismantle unearned income from speculation and ensure equity in wealth distribution, addressing systemic inequality rooted in historical land grabs and exclusion.

II. Efficiency: A Non-Distortionary Engine for Growth

Unlike income, sales, or corporate taxes—which deter work, investment, and consumption—LVT is uniquely non-distortionary. Since land cannot be produced or moved, taxing it does not reduce its supply. Instead, it incentivizes efficient land use: underutilized urban lots would either be developed or sold to those who will, curbing speculation and urban blight. Cities like Pittsburgh and towns in Pennsylvania that adopted LVT in the 20th century saw revitalized downtowns, increased construction activity, and reduced housing vacancies, proving its efficacy.

Moreover, LVT mitigates the deadweight loss inherent in conventional taxation. By eliminating taxes on productive activity, labor and capital are freed to innovate and circulate, boosting economic dynamism. Landowners, unburdened by taxes on improvements, invest in greener, more resilient infrastructure, while tenants benefit from lower rents as landlords compete to attract occupants. This efficiency extends ecologically: compact urban development spurred by LVT curtails sprawl, preserving natural habitats and reducing carbon footprints.

III. Sufficiency: A Robust Sole Revenue Source

Critics argue that LVT alone cannot fund public services, yet data suggests otherwise. A 2019 study estimated that capturing 100% of land rent in the U.S. could generate up to $1.3 trillion annually, exceeding total state and local government revenue. In Denmark, land value taxation has long underpinned public finance, while Namibia’s partial LVT reduced urban poverty by 17%. By abolishing redundant taxes and tapping into the vast, untapped reservoir of land rents—particularly in high-value urban areas—governments can fully fund essential services without compromising growth.

Replacing regressive sales taxes and payroll levies with LVT would also lighten the burden on low- and middle-income households. Unlike income or property taxes, which disproportionately strain earners and homeowners, LVT targets those best positioned to pay: land speculators and absentee landlords. This realignment fosters a more progressive fiscal system where wealth is measured not by labor or consumption but by the privilege of land ownership.

Opponents raise three key concerns: valuation accuracy, rural applicability, and transition challenges. Yet modern appraisal techniques—leveraging big data, location analytics, and comparable sales—already enable precise land valuation. Rural land, valued for its potential use, would incur lower taxes than prime urban sites, reflecting its modest market value. Transitional justice is addressed by phasing in LVT gradually, allowing landowners to adapt while compensating those unfairly affected by sudden policy shifts.

Claims that LVT discourages landownership ignore its neutrality: owners profit from improvements, untaxed, while paying only for the privilege of location. Unlike income or sales taxes, LVT cannot be evaded by relocating capital or labor, making it both unavoidable and stable—a critical trait for public finance.

Conclusion

The Georgist vision of a 100% land value tax transcends partisan divides, offering a path to a fairer, more dynamic economy. By reclaiming land rent as a collective asset, we dismantle inequality, spur innovation, and align fiscal policy with ecological sustainability. As cities worldwide grapple with housing crises, climate change, and stagnant growth, LVT stands not as a radical experiment but as a return to first principles: that the earth’s bounty belongs equally to all, and that public revenue should spring not from toil or trade, but from the land we share. The time has come to embrace this timeless truth.

Title: The Case for a 100% Land Value Tax: Unlocking Fairness, Efficiency, and Prosperity

The idea that the earth belongs to all is an ancient moral truth, appearing in philosophies from Aristotle to Abraham Lincoln. In the late 19th century, the political economist Henry George gave this timeless principle an economic structure: a land value tax on the unimproved value of land—a levy not on what people produce, but on the natural value of location, soil, minerals, and other benefits of the earth that no individual created. Today, we can advance this idea further: implementing a 100% Land Value Tax (LVT) on the unimproved value of land, fully capturing land rent for the public, while abolishing all taxes on labor and productive capital. This reform would be morally just, economically efficient, and the most practical strategy for eliminating poverty and unearned monopoly.

I. The Moral Argument: Why Land Rent Belongs to the People

Land, unlike human-made goods, is not a product of labor. No individual created the soil, the coastline, the mineral deposits, or the central street corner. The value of a plot in New York or San Francisco is largely the product of location advantages created by the community and public investment—roads, schools, safety, transit—not the efforts of the individual landowner.

When private owners capture land’s rising value, they reap rewards for merely holding a deed, not for creating wealth. This is the foundation of economic rent—income without productive contribution. A 100% tax on this unearned rent is not a confiscation of someone’s labor; it is a restoration to the public of wealth the public created. Anything less than full capture allows some individuals to privatize value that rightly belongs to all, generating inequality and speculative windfalls for a few at the expense of the many.

By eliminating all other taxes and sourcing revenue solely from land rent, society acknowledges an essential moral distinction: we own what we produce, but we share what nature provides.

II. The Efficiency Argument: Ending Waste and Unlocking Productivity

Unlike taxes on income, sales, or buildings—which discourage work, trade, and improvement—a land value tax is economically non-distortionary. You cannot hide land, and you cannot reduce its supply in response to taxation. By taxing the unimproved value only, we leave all incentive to develop, build, and innovate intact. In fact, fully taxing land values encourages productive use by removing incentives for speculation and hoarding.

Under the current system, speculators frequently hold valuable vacant lots in high-demand cities, waiting for their value to appreciate while contributing nothing. A 100% LVT makes such practices unprofitable. Landholders must either develop their land to generate income to pay the tax, or sell it to someone who will. As a result, we would see an end to artificial scarcity, more affordable housing, and greater employment as underutilized sites are put to their highest purpose.

Economic studies and historical data—from the Hong Kong leasehold system to land tax reforms in parts of Australia and Pennsylvania—consistently show that land-based taxation increases urban vitality, reduces sprawl, and stimulates investment in productive enterprise instead of destructive speculation.

III. The Fiscal Argument: A Self-Sustaining, Single-Tax Society

Henry George envisioned the Single Tax: the full collection of land rent as the sole source of government revenue. Some argue that only partial land taxation is feasible, but in reality the aggregate annual rental value of land is vast—often underestimated.

In developed economies, total land rents can equal 20–30% or more of GDP. This would be more than sufficient to fund core government functions, infrastructure, public goods, and even a citizens’ dividend. By shifting entirely to LVT and abolishing taxes on wages, sales, and capital, we would free labor and enterprise from the deadweight costs of taxation. The wealth that accrues naturally from the common heritage—the surface of the earth—would flow back to fund common needs.

This approach eliminates the bureaucracy of income and corporate tax enforcement, reduces loopholes and evasion, and ties government revenue directly to the health and efficiency of land use, creating a virtuous fiscal circle: the more we as a community enhance the value of a location, the more our public treasury grows.

IV. Addressing Common Objections

Critics worry that a 100% LVT would be confiscatory, discouraging ownership or harming the economy. This misreads the nature of what is taxed. The LVT does not seize the products of labor or capital—it only collects the annual rental value of a resource we all share. Owners would still reap the full benefit of their own improvements, but not the unearned windfall from societal progress.

Some argue it would hurt farmers or rural landowners. In fact, since rural land values are far lower than urban ones, the tax burden would primarily fall on wealthy holders of high-value urban land. Farmers would pay far less under a pure LVT than under current income or sales tax regimes, while benefiting from better infrastructure and reduced costs for goods and services.

V. The Broader Social Vision

A 100% LVT isn’t just economic reform—it’s a democratic rebalancing of our relationship with one another and with the earth. By returning land rent to public purposes, we dismantle the structural privilege that turns landownership into a guaranteed path to wealth regardless of effort, and we replace it with a just baseline: what you earn from your own labor is yours to keep; what you gain from society belongs to society.

This transition would spur a renaissance. Freed from the burden of taxes on productivity, entrepreneurs could innovate without penalty. Cities would redevelop sustainably. Speculative bubbles in real estate—a driver of economic cycles and crashes—would be deflated permanently. Poverty would lose its material root, as access to land opportunities would expand.

Conclusion: A Bold, Just, and Practical Reform

The 100% land value tax, as envisioned by Georgist economic philosophy, is more than another fiscal tweak—it is the structural reform needed for a fair, efficient, and prosperous society. Land is the birthright of all; its value is the product of collective activity and must be shared collectively. By fully capturing land rent and abolishing all taxes on labor and capital, we create a tax system that is just in principle, efficient in practice, and sufficient for the needs of civilization.

It is time to replace unjust taxation with a revenue system rooted in moral truth and economic sense. The earth is the common inheritance of humanity; the rent it yields should serve humanity as a whole. The 100% Land Value Tax is not only fair—it is the key to an economy where opportunity is truly universal, and where prosperity arises from contribution, not privilege.

The Moral and Economic Imperative of a Pure Land Value Tax

Introduction: The Forgotten Revolution in Political Economy

In an era defined by staggering inequality, speculative asset bubbles, and governments struggling to fund essential services without stifling productive enterprise, the answers to our fiscal and social crises may lie not in novel innovation but in a revolutionary idea from the 19th century. Henry George, in his seminal work Progress and Poverty, diagnosed the core ailment of industrial society with brilliant clarity and proposed a remedy of radical simplicity: abolish all taxes on labor and capital, and instead raise all public revenue from a single tax on the unimproved value of land. This essay argues that the full implementation of a 100% Land Value Tax (LVT)—capturing the entire economic rent of land for public benefit—is not only a just and efficient policy but the only logical foundation for a prosperous, fair, and dynamic society.

Part I: The Moral Imperative – Justice and the Common Heritage

The case for a pure LVT rests first and foremost on a profound moral truth: the earth is the common inheritance of all people. Its value—the location, the fertility, the mineral deposits, the access to markets and communities—is not created by the landholder. It is created by society as a whole. The value of a plot in downtown Tokyo or Manhattan is not a product of its owner’s labor but of the collective investment in infrastructure, the density of population, the network of commerce, and the cultural vitality of the city. When a government builds a subway station, the surrounding land values soar, and the landowner reaps a windfall for doing nothing more than holding a deed.

To permit private individuals to capture this socially created value is the fundamental injustice George identified. It is a privatization of the commons, a "robbery" as he termed it. A 100% LVT is, therefore, the mechanism of restitution. It collects the rent due to the community and returns it for common benefit—funding schools, hospitals, defense, and environmental stewardship. It rectifies the ancient wrong of allowing a privileged few to levy a "tribute" on others for the mere privilege of using what belongs to all. This is not confiscation; it is the collection of a debt owed. It aligns the legal framework with the philosophical truth that no one made the land, and thus no one should have an exclusive claim to its unimproved value.

Part II: The Economic Imperative – Efficiency and Dynamism

Beyond justice, a pure LVT is the most efficient possible tax. Modern economics recognizes that taxes distort behavior. Taxes on income discourage work. Taxes on capital gains discourage investment. Taxes on buildings discourage maintenance and improvement. These are "deadweight losses"—economic activities suppressed by the tax that would otherwise benefit everyone.

The tax on land value is uniquely free from this flaw. The supply of land, in an economic sense, is perfectly fixed. It cannot be created or destroyed in response to a tax. You cannot move your plot to another jurisdiction to avoid it. Therefore, a tax on its value cannot reduce the supply or create scarcity. It does not discourage anyone from using land; indeed, it encourages efficient use. An LVT forces the market to price land according to its highest and best use. The owner of a blighted, vacant lot in a thriving city center, who currently speculates by waiting for values to rise while contributing nothing, will face a tax bill that makes such holding economically untenable. They must either develop it productively, sell it to someone who will, or forfeit the holding to the state. This ends speculative land-banking, the practice that starves cities of needed housing and commerce. It channels capital into productive enterprise—building homes, factories, and shops—rather than into unproductive rent-seeking.

By shifting the entire tax burden from the factors of production (labor and capital) to the passive, unearned factor (land rent), we unleash the economy’s productive power. Entrepreneurs keep more of what they earn; workers take home fuller paychecks. The tax base grows as the economy becomes more dynamic. This is the efficient engine George envisioned: a state funded by its own natural resource, leaving the fruits of industry to circulate freely.

Part III: The Practical Imperative – Solving the Intractable Problems

The practical applications of a pure LVT solve today’s most intractable problems.

1. The Housing Crisis: Soaring home prices are not primarily a shortage of bricks and mortar but a crisis of land costs. An LVT crashes the speculative premium on land, making development for housing financially rational. It shifts incentives from "buy and hold" to "build and provide."

2. Inequality: Land ownership is the most concentrated form of wealth. The billionaire’s portfolio often relies heavily on appreciating land holdings. An LVT directly targets unearned, unproductive wealth, reducing inequality more effectively than income taxes while encouraging the rich to invest their capital in job-creating ventures instead of rent-collection.

3. Government Integrity and Simplicity: A single tax is simple to administer. Land values are observable, relatively stable, and do not require intrusive investigations into private affairs. It reduces the lobbying for exemptions and loopholes that plague complex tax codes. Furthermore, because LVT revenue is tied to the land value itself, local government funding naturally aligns with the public investments that increase that value, creating a virtuous cycle of civic improvement.

Part IV: Rebutting the Objections

Opponents raise predictable concerns. "It would hurt farmers and the middle class who own their land!" This is a misunderstanding. The LVT falls on the unimproved value of the land—the bare land price. The farmhouse, barns, and improvements are exempt. A farmer who owns valuable land in a growing city would owe a high tax, but that is a signal of the immense wealth embedded in their asset. They could borrow against that wealth to pay the tax, or sell some land to a developer who would use it intensively, securing a capital sum for their retirement. The policy does not create poverty; it reveals latent wealth.

"Land value is difficult to assess." This is a technical, not a fundamental, problem. Modern assessment techniques, based on comparable sales and land-value estimation models (separating land from improvement value), are well-established. The challenge is political will, not technical feasibility.

"It’s radical and has never been fully tried." This is an argument for timidity, not truth. Elements of LVT exist in successful jurisdictions worldwide, such as parts of Pennsylvania (with notably more vibrant downtowns), Singapore, Denmark, and Estonia. The full implementation would be revolutionary because our current system is so deeply entrenched in injustice and inefficiency. The status quo’s failure to address inequality, housing, and productivity is not a reason to abandon a proven solution; it is the reason to embrace it.

Conclusion: A Moral Mandate for a Modern Age

Henry George’s proposal is not an arcane relic of 19th-century radicalism. It is a prescient diagnosis of the chronic diseases of capitalism and a coherent, powerful cure. A 100% Land Value Tax is the embodiment of a simple principle: people should own the fruits of their labor and ingenuity, but the value of the earth—which is nobody’s labor—belongs to everyone.

To implement it fully would be to declare that our society values productive work over passive speculation, common benefit over private privilege, and economic dynamism over stagnant rent-seeking. It would unleash a cascade of development, slash inequality, and fund a generous state not through coercion of the productive but through the reclaiming of what is already ours. The path forward is not to find new taxes to burden the industrious, but to stop letting the luckiest among us charge us all rent for the ground beneath our feet. The unimproved value of land is the common treasury, and it is time we acted like it.

3. Reduced Rent-Seeking and Inequality

  • Land ownership concentrates wealth passively. Owners capture "unearned income" — gains they didn't create.
  • By redirecting this value to public use, Georgists argue society reduces the gap between those who produce and those who merely own.
